articles.title: Pittsburgh’s ‘Green Man’ was a real person – why the legend outlives the facts
articles.author: Jeffrey Tolbert, Associate Professor of American Studies and Folklore, Penn State
paras: Every semester I teach a class called History of Monsters, Aliens and the Supernatural at Penn State. It fills up quickly, because students, like many people, are fascinated by the supernatural.
During the course, students occasionally bring up the western Pennsylvania tradition of the “Green Man.”
As a folklorist, I study the traditions people practice and share in everyday life, from jokes and family recipes to birthday customs and ghost stories.
The story of the Green Man shows how legends and history can tangle – and how each person who retells a legend helps remake it.
What makes a legend a legend

In everyday speech, “legend” often means a story that isn’t true. For folklorists, a legend is a story about something that may have happened in the real world, told as if it could be true but always open to debate.

As Linda Dégh, a prominent Hungarian American folklorist, once put it, “The legend is a legend once it entertains debate about belief. … The sounding of contrary opinions is what makes a legend a legend.”
This is in contrast to myths, for example, which are sacred creation or explanatory stories set before or outside of normal time.

Importantly, myths and legends are not simply false narratives. They contain different kinds of truth, which depend on the perspectives of the people sharing them. Folklorists don’t study such stories in order to disprove them. Our goal is to understand why these stories matter to people.

Legends are distinct from history because they do not center on established, generally agreed-upon facts about past events. They are more like contested historical narratives that may at times align with consensus history and at other times subvert it.
The real man behind the Green Man

According to news coverage, the man at the center of this legend, Raymond Robinson, was 8 years old in 1919 when he climbed a bridge near Beaver Falls, in Beaver County, Pennsylvania, to reach a bird’s nest and touched a live electrical line. He survived, but lost his eyes, nose and part of an arm.

Robinson lived with his family in nearby Koppel. To avoid attention, as the legend goes, he took to walking along a quiet stretch of Route 351 at night. Some called him “Charlie No-Face,” but “Green Man” seems to have caught on among people from farther away.
A number of people claimed to have met and spoken with him directly during his nighttime walks. Some who met him were kind to him, news outlets reported; others, less so. Robinson died in 1985.

A reporter from the Post-Gazette suggests that the truly frightening part of the story is how Robinson became an object of fear and ridicule. In a KDKA report, Robinson’s great-niece describes him as an exceptionally kind person. And PennLive reporter Claudia Dimuro writes, “But maybe in between seeking these thrills from supposed ghosts lurking in abandoned tunnels, we should stop and wonder whether they were once someone real.”

The “thrills” Dimuro refers to stem from a practice folklorists call legend-tripping – that is, deliberately visiting a location associated with a legend, often in order to experience some part of the legend for oneself.

These articles note that many people deliberately set out to visit Robinson while he lived and went on his nighttime walks. While it might be tempting to assume that an encounter with a real human being would end the supernatural legend of the Green Man, these real-life encounters may have actually bolstered the legend.
Legend, truth, fiction, fact

Popular media coverage of folklore often tries to debunk it. The Discovery Channel show “MythBusters” was built around testing popular beliefs, such as whether a penny dropped from the Empire State Building could kill someone. Many news articles about the Green Man also engage in debunking by highlighting the real life of the man behind the legend. That urge makes sense, especially when false claims can hurt real people. Casting Robinson as a monster dehumanizes a man who lived with severe disabilities, and his family still lives with that legacy.

Legends occupy an unstable place between fiction and reality. Robinson was real, and so were his nighttime walks. But the Green Man of legend – a glowing, threatening figure with supernatural powers who supposedly lived in a tunnel – was not. The so-called Green Man Tunnel in South Park Township seems to have had nothing to do with Robinson’s actual life.
Still, people “really” met the “real” Green Man, and those meetings, for better or for worse, contributed to the legend. Instead of laying it to rest, those encounters likely helped preserve it.

I doubt that debunking the supernatural or monstrous parts of the Green Man legend will make it fade away. Still, I’m sympathetic to the desire to honor the real man at the heart of the story, and to push back on the dehumanization and ableism that drew such interest to his story in the first place. And the link between the monstrous legend and Robinson’s real life is itself a historical matter. Robinson was a real person who really became the central figure of a legend. To fully tell his history means acknowledging that legend as part of it.

Legends are, after all, talk about a supposed past. As a form of talk, legends persist as long as we continue talking about them. But legends are by definition debatable, their claims are never solid, and they’re never really on stable ground.

If, in the future, students bring up the Green Man in my Monsters class, I’ll acknowledge that, yes, this is an example of a legend. It features a man made into a kind of monster. I’ll note that legends, as talk about things that may have happened and people who may have been, are never neutral.

But I’ll also suggest that, because legends are debatable, unstable and contested, there’s always room for us to challenge and correct problematic claims when we hear them, and to bring humanity to stories unjustly focused on monstrosity. We can, if we choose to, tell a different version of the story.

articles.title: AI may quickly generate ideas, but working with people leads to more creative ones
articles.author: Clin Lai, Postdoctoral Fellow in Artificial Intelligence and Society, Brandeis University
paras: The productivity gains of generative AI are often touted as the main reason for its rapid adoption. Much like how a calculator can instantly solve mathematical equations too long for the human brain to compute, generative AI can help someone quickly summarize long articles and draft emails.
But beyond productivity, a key question remains: How is AI affecting quintessentially human activities, such as collaboration and creativity?
As cognitive scientists who study creativity, we recently conducted an experiment that explored how working with AI – rather than humans – affects originality and other aspects of creativity.
Speedy and wordy doesn’t mean creative

Creativity is often tied to what cognitive scientists call “divergent thinking.” One way of measuring divergent thinking is to ask someone to come up with a range of uses for a common item, such as a brick or a book. This is known as the alternate uses task.
Researchers then compare the number of ideas and the originality of these ideas to assess creative capacity.

Large language models appear to have the “number of ideas” part down pat: They can generate many more ideas than humans can. This ability to produce more – and produce that high volume more quickly – partially explains why more than half of new articles online are now generated by AI.

These texts, however, are often verbose, with redundant information. Researchers who tested 12 AI chatbots across different companies on thousands of factual questions found that their answers were often many times longer than human-written answers, with the actual answer making up only about 42% of the text. The rest was largely extra padding: repetitive information, unnecessary background details and explanations that went into too much detail or veered off topic.
Large language models also seem to struggle with the originality of their outputs.
An ‘original’ idea – again and again

In our research, we compared the results of people working on the alternate uses task with another person to those who collaborated with ChatGPT on the same task. We randomly assigned 208 participants to work with either AI or another person.

We found that compared with two people taking turns together, people working with ChatGPT wrote longer responses on the alternate uses task. But human pairs came up with more creative ideas than the humans working with ChatGPT.

We also found that the ideas people came up with when working with other people tended to be more distinct and diverse than those who worked with large language models. Individual AI suggestions could be quite creative – using a book as a sound dampener, for example – but ChatGPT presented that same idea across many separate sessions, making its overall pool of ideas more homogeneous.

Other studies have highlighted the homogeneity of generative AI’s outputs. One group of researchers found that using AI repeatedly over time to generate images often results in bland, generic pictures – what they call “visual elevator music.” Other studies have found that although AI may help an individual write a more creative story when compared with their preexisting work, AI-assisted writing as a whole, across all users, tends to be more similar.

All of this makes sense when you think about how large language models work. After being trained on massive sets of texts, large language models predict the next most likely words. Because their training processes were similar, different large language models, whether it’s ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, tend to have similar cadences, diction, syntax and suggestions – particularly when compared with the work of two random human writers.
In other words, generative AI’s ideas may seem unique in a vacuum. But if everyone’s using AI, the ideas and writing style start to converge.
Creative collaboration is a long game
Finally, we also found that the creativity benefits of working with another person became even stronger as the collaboration progressed.

Ideas can be measured through semantic distance, which is a way of quantifying how distinct individual concepts are. Over time, interacting with other humans seems to result in larger semantic distance than interacting with a chatbot. In other words, people may traverse more creative terrain when collaborating with other people. Meanwhile, the tendency for ideas to converge in chatbot-assisted brainstorming could accumulate, potentially narrowing the range of ideas people explore over the course of a long period of time.
This is important because many creative projects involve long-term engagement.

For example, to launch a new product, researchers have found that it takes an average of 27 months to go from the initial idea to the finished product. More innovative products can take as long as 54 months.
Chat-human before you ChatGPT
If you want to work with a chatbot, how can you preserve your creativity in the face of AI’s tendency toward homogeneity?

Some research suggests using what’s called “persona prompting.” Like talking to other people with different perspectives, users could provide an extensive prompt to give chatbots a pretend personality that can simulate different types of people. For example, you might prompt it to respond as if it is “a male college professor from India who is an expert in teaching” or “a 58-year-old female founder of a construction company.” Researchers found that while this persona prompting increased ChatGPT’s idea diversity, the overall range of ideas still fell short of that produced by human writers. These findings echo other recent research suggesting that chatbots are poor simulators of human personality.

If you need help with a creative task, we suggest going back to the basics: Chat with a person before chatting with AI. They’ll have idiosyncratic personal experiences that can’t be captured by a large language model that’s trained to generate average responses.

Composing a sentence, however modest, is a creative act, whether it’s in a text to a friend or a wedding speech. As AI is integrated into workflows, it’s important to remember that other people can still be a valuable resource. Work completed in collaboration with other humans feels more meaningful.
They might not respond as quickly or as comprehensively. But chances are they’ll have something more interesting to say.

articles.title: Five ways to find your personal style outside of trends and algorithms
articles.author: Rose Davison, Senior Lecturer in Fashion Marketing, Management and Communication, Nottingham Trent University
paras: Fashion is currently trapped in a hyper-accelerated trend loop. Every week there’s a new “core” or “maxxing” style to contend with – such as balletcore or whimsymaxxing. They zoom in and out of our cultural consciousness with alarming speed.

These fads are so numerous that we can be confounded with choice, so oddly specific that we need a new wardrobe to be part of them, and so rapid that there is rarely time to understand or assimilate our own style preferences.

In 1937 the author, critic and art historian James Laver developed Laver’s law, charting how clothing styles evolve in public perception over a 160-year cycle. He asserted that clothing was seen as “charming” after 70 years, but “ridiculous” after just 20.

Yet today, 1990s and Y2K fashion dominate consumer trends. At first glance, this speed-run of recent history appears to clash with the weekly conveyor belt of TikTok micro-trends. In reality, they are two sides of the same algorithmic phenomenon.

Rather than cycling through distinct eras sequentially as Laver predicted, social media feeds flatten time entirely. Decades of vintage subcultures and instant micro-aesthetics are collapsed into the same endless scroll, allowing a 1990s minimalist silhouette to coexist alongside a week-old “whimsymaxxing” viral trend.
Having lived through both the 1990s and Y2K style moments the first time around, it is clear they are also defying Laver’s timeline – they remain far from “ridiculous” to younger generations.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
Social media hasn’t killed personal style, it’s killed how we communicate it
A brief history of embroidery – and how to get started yourself
Indie sleaze: a brief fashion history, from messy rebellion to mainstream revival

In Fashion: A Philosophy (2004), the Norwegian philosopher Lars Svendsen described how the “traditional replacement logic of fashion […] has itself been replaced by a logic of supplementation”. Rather than a style coming in and going out of vogue, we now continuously accumulate more styles – produced and consumed faster than ever before.

This shift is driven not only by the speed of online micro-trends, but by mass accessibility and algorithmic marketing. If you feel overwhelmed by the choice and density of the clothing that is around us, that’s probably because at no other time have we been surrounded by so much stuff and had so many possibilities marketed at us. As psychologist Barry Schwartz examines in his book The Paradox of Choice (2016), an overabundance of choice – whether on high street shelves or digital feeds – ultimately causes demoralisation rather than liberation.

Consider the barrage of styles that have recently dominated social feeds. Whether it is the viral “mob wife” or “brat” aesthetics or the heralded return of “indie sleaze”, consumers are inundated with manufactured novelty.

These “must-haves” do not emerge to fill genuine human need. Does the environment truly require us to “whimsymaxx” our way to the nearest landfill? This rapid turnover exploits our impulses – provoking a knee-jerk reaction to buy new goods to avoid feeling outdated.

Paradoxically, recent trends such as normcore, dadcore and gorpcore seem to revel in an “anti-style” aesthetic – prioritising utility and nonchalance over a fashion statement. Yet even these styles require consumer participation. Technical gear designed for extreme outdoor survival from heritage performance brands like Arc'teryx and Gore-Tex is repackaged as high-fashion streetwear, attached to considerable price tags, and pushed through the exact same hyper-accelerated promotional machinery.
Developing an authentic personal style amid this constant marketing can feel daunting. But there are ways to turn down the noise and reclaim your sartorial agency.

Look to figures whose attitude and expression transcend trends – whether it is the uncompromising tailoring worn by Lauren Bacall, the unabashed classicism of Paul Newman or the eclecticism of contemporary stylist Catherine Baba.

Looking back to past eras – before commercial algorithms and fast-fashion feeds dictated daily wear – reveals how individuals curated distinct personal styles. They relied on craftsmanship, silhouette and their personal eccentricities, rather than algorithmic prompts.
2. Reevaluate where, when and what you buy

It sounds daft, but only buy things you actually like. It’s difficult to not enjoy getting dressed when you are choosing from garments that you bought because they make you happy. Go into charity shops and vintage shops and see what you are drawn to in a space where there is (slightly) less trend interference.
3. Think about your messaging
Consider what your wardrobe communicates about your character. Are those puffed sleeved, smocked, tiered dresses really a match for a steely personality, for example?
Evaluate whether transient high-street silhouettes align with your actual lifestyle and self-image, or if they merely reflect passing promotional campaigns.

Look to personal or family archives – photographs of parents, grandparents or historical eras – to identify timeless silhouettes and durable materials that offer a real alternative to influencer-driven fast fashion. If your mum looked great in a ribbed polo neck, there’s a strong chance you will too.
Clever styling, repairing, dyeing and managing your wardrobe can help you to see that what you have is probably enough.

The commercial landscape we live in always tells us we need the latest this and the newest that but, as Schwartz examines in The Paradox of Choice, having the extravagance of choice present in shops and online, actually does us harm.
Breaking away from the feeds, the reels, the ads and the algorithm will mean you can curate a less dictated sense of style – and have a wardrobe that truly speaks to who you are.

articles.title: Primetime: in this taut morally complex thriller, ambition, entertainment and justice collide
articles.author: Laura O'Flanagan, PhD Candidate, School of English, Dublin City University
paras: Director Lance Oppenheim creates a grim and grubby world in Primetime, steeped in the sweat and compromised ambitions of its characters. But below the film’s grimy surface is a sharp examination of the personal and professional concessions people make in pursuit of success.

Inspired by real events, Primetime follows American television presenter Chris Hansen (Robert Pattinson), whose NBC reality TV series To Catch a Predator became a ratings sensation between 2004 and 2007.

The film is set in 2006 as Hansen, working with producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever), oversees sting operations. In the set-up, men are lured into houses believing they are meeting underage children, only to be confronted by Hansen and his cameras.

Among those recruited is aspiring actor Dan Plum (Skyler Gisondo) as TV bait, whose involvement offers another perspective on the enterprise. Pattinson’s performance as Hansen carefully reveals the deep insecurity beneath his relentless ambition. Constantly comparing himself with more successful figures, Hansen is consumed by a desire for fame and recognition.

At times Pattinson appears almost reptilian, observing those around him with a cold, calculating intensity. Hanson’s commitment to exposing wrongdoing becomes increasingly difficult to separate from his determination to make a name for himself. There is something distinctly predatory about his pursuit of success, troubling the neat division between predator and prey on which To Catch a Predator depends.

Wever is excellent as the harried Bender, whose commitment to the project and qualms about its ethics seem curiously dependent on its success. She treads the line between the pressures of keeping the programme afloat and the ease with which moral reservations give way to professional ambition.

Gisondo is impressive as “Decoy Dan”, bringing a tightly controlled earnestness to an aspiring actor who sees the sting operations as a career opportunity. His vulnerability during the first encounter also exposes reality TV’s potential to cause harm.

Oppenheim’s background in documentary filmmaking informs Primetime’s visual approach. The security footage and VHS-style imagery lend the film a rough authenticity which evokes the television of the mid 2000s.

Period details, such as popular drama Lost as a ratings rival, reinforce this sense of time and place. And the curious appearance of former NBC executive Jeff Zucker as himself, among a cast of actors portraying real-life figures, further blurs the distinction between fiction and documentary.

The surveillance footage also places viewers in the uncomfortable position of watching the sting operations unfold, making us participants in the spectacle of exposure. To Catch a Predator effectively appointed itself judge and jury, voyeuristically subjecting suspected sexual predators to public humiliation in the name of protecting children.

Oppenheim explores the uneasy morality of an enterprise whose targets draw hatred and anger even as its methods invite scrutiny. By drawing us into these encounters, he raises questions about our own responsibility as viewers. We are, after all, consuming the very entertainment whose ethics the film calls into question.

It has been a remarkable year for Oppenheim, whose Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, co-directed with Nathan Fielder, has become an unlikely US box-office hit. The film took more than $45 million (£34m) in its first ten days. Both films suggest a fascination with controversial public figures and the uncomfortable questions surrounding their pursuit of success.

In Primetime, this produces a seedy, unsettling portrait of ambition, anchored by excellent performances and a distinctive visual approach. Its interest in the people behind the cameras extends to those watching, implicating the audience in the spectacle it depicts.
The film leaves us to consider how easily the pursuit of justice can become a form of exploitation, and what responsibility we bear for the entertainment we consume.

articles.title: Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon-stealing spirits
articles.author: Alex Brown, Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University
paras: Stories of wandering spirits and the restless dead were common in the Middle Ages. These ghostly encounters were recorded in a wide variety of medieval literature.

Medieval ghost stories combined folklore traditions with religious doctrine. The widespread belief in purgatory – a place where souls were cleansed of sin before entering heaven – helped fuel the belief in ghosts.

Spirits of the departed were thought able to return, exhorting the living to pray for them and make amends on their behalf to aid their passage through purgatory. As a result, medieval ghost stories often contained a strong moral and religious message.

Historians have long been fascinated by a series of 12 ghost stories written down in the early years of the 15th century at Byland Abbey, a Cistercian monastery in north Yorkshire. They recorded a bizarre and eclectic array of ghosts, featuring shape-shifting spirits, miracle stories and the walking dead, who crept up on the living.

These tales were clearly intended to scare people. They referred to the “terrors of the night” and to spirits rising from their graves to “disturb and terrify villagers”. One graphically described a woman sinking her hand into a spirit’s flesh as if it were rotten and insubstantial.

Some of those who encountered these spirits were even said to have been hurt or fallen “ill and languished for many days” afterwards. Yet the primary aim of most of the ghosts was not to physically harm the living. In one story, a spirit threw a man over a hedge but then caught him on the other side so he did not get hurt. Instead, ghosts most often sought the help of the living.

In one of the stories, two men were walking in a field when suddenly one fled “in great terror” as the other man was “left struggling with a spirit who badly tore his clothes”. The man managed to “conjure” the ghost – a vital step enabling the living and dead to communicate. The ghost then confessed that he had been excommunicated for stealing silver spoons. He begged the man to restore the spoons and request absolution on his behalf, which he duly did.

Such stories were intended to be instructive. The reader was encouraged to think about others who might be in purgatory, and to pray for their salvation. They were also exhorted to consider their own behaviour and to amend their ways before their own demise.

Some of the stories made this explicit. In one which revolved around a real inheritance dispute, the sister of Adam de London, a minor landowner in Ampleforth, was compelled to wander the village after her death. She explicitly threatened her brother that if he did not restore the disputed property to her husband and sons, he would suffer the same fate as her upon his death.

Some of these moral messages are timeless, but others clearly conveyed the concerns of medieval landowners. In one story, a poor spirit was being “grievously punished” because he had not ploughed his master’s land sufficiently well.

Religious faith was vital in confronting such spectral visitors. In one story, a man named William de Bradeforth was followed by a ghost crying “how, how, how”. William commanded the spirit to depart “in the name of the Lord and by the power of the blood of Jesus Christ”. The ghost was said to flee, “looking like a piece of canvas unfurling its four corners and billowing away”.

In another, a spirit appeared to a tailor called “Snowball” in various forms, including a raven and a dog. The spirit admitted that he only had the power to visit the man because he had not heard Mass that day.

Sometimes the moral instruction in such stories was less clear. For example, the revenant of James Tankerlay, a former rector, came forth and blinded his former concubine. No one sought to communicate with him or put him to rest. Instead, they opted for banishing the ghost by digging up his corpse and throwing his remains into a mire.
This echoes earlier stories of revenants and the walking dead. In this tradition, the return of the dead could be prevented by beheading, burning or otherwise mutilating the bodies of the deceased.

Archaeological evidence suggests this may not have been just a literary invention but was occasionally carried out. Skeletons from between the 11th and 13th centuries at the deserted medieval village of Wharram Percy in north Yorkshire had a series of post-mortem mutilations that may have reflected such anxieties around the walking dead.
Living an upright life might have promised peace in heaven, but when it came to keeping the dead in their graves, medieval communities clearly preferred not to take any chances.
Alex Brown is currently the Principal Investigator of a Leverhulme Trust funded project on 'Modelling the Black Death'.

articles.title: Hailed as a 21st-century Greek masterpiece, Gjak retains its bloody power in English translation
articles.author: Gonda Van Steen, Koraes Chair of Modern Greek and Byzantine History, Language and Literature, King's College London
paras: Blood is the word. Blood in every sense. Gjak: Tales of Blood, written by Dimosthenis Papamarkos, was a massive success on publication in 2014. It won the prestigious Academy of Athens award and has become one of the most widely discussed works of 21st-century Greek literature.
Now it has found its perfect voice in English in the 2026 translation by Siân Valvis, a British-Greek literary translator working across Greek, Russian, French and Portuguese.

With her translation of Gjak, Valvis has now also successfully navigated the language and ethos of the Arvanite villages. The Arvanites are a bilingual group, descendants of migrants from Albania in the 13th to 16th centuries who settled in central and southern Greece. Their language, Arvanitic, is an Albanian dialect seasoned with loans from other languages and dialects.
Gjak was written in a dialect blending elements of Arvanitic into Greek. Valvis’s English translation is startling: a vivid, at times raw, at times highly lyrical text.

As an expert in the trauma of 20th-century Greek warfare, the weight of cultural memory and the complex historical identity of the Arvanite people, seldom have I read a work that exudes so much linguistic and cultural ruggedness and sensitivity all at once. I came away with a sense of uneasy familiarity and I am sure you will too, for there is no place to hide from the bloodlines and trails that link us all.

Gjak is series of interconnected short stories, which strive to portray what ordinary life was like remote villages that had become more Greek as they were formalised as part of the Greek nation state. Each explores what it was like living in the aftermath of the Greco-Turkish wars of 1919 to 1922.

With Greek and Arvanite soldiers returning to their villages, peace – internal as well as external – should have had a real chance at being restored. No such thing. These warriors carry blood and guilt with them and these infiltrate deeply into blood lines, family and fraternal bonds, love and homoerotic relationships, village and community dynamics, even relations across borders and oceans (to reach the diaspora communities of the New World).

Blood and the guilt associated with death become the proverbial red threads tying Papamarkos’s short stories together. These connected bloody threads are also revealed in the ballad-style poem that functions as an intermezzo at the book’s midway point. This ballad is not an interlude of lightness. It is, rather, the lyric tale of a courageous woman’s encounter with bloodthirsty Death himself. With this ballad, too, the female voice appears loud and strong in the text and in the translation. Women are subjects in most of the stories otherwise, strong though they may be – and certainly no strangers to blood and violence.

Valvis’s translation does these bloody threads justice at every turn. The work here pushes at the boundaries of literature, linguistics, history and nationalism. But even more so, the translator has unflinchingly portrayed PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). Papamarkos does not hold back when describing how victims of PTSD behave, with continued violence that can turn very visceral, and Valvis has managed to translate this vividly and sensitively.

Thankfully, the translator carefully explains in a note what is at stake, what choices she has made and what the trajectory of the translation has been (a five-year-long process for a book of about 140 pages).

Valvis’s unsettlingly direct language succeeds in having the readers question themselves. Can we write off violence and revenge as belonging to others or are we complicit too? The character aptly called the “knocker” explains, in Valvis’s deliberately ironic (misspelled) language and grammar:

Folk don’t mind foulness so long as it stays out of sight and it’s not their hands getting dirty. So long as they can go out, dressed up, arm in arm wi their lady friends, free of stink, and pick up cutlery with hands that aren’t swollen with blood and tuck into their steak without getting dirty. That’s what it means to be sivilized. Stepping on shit in high heels. It’s hidden, the work I do at Union, just like what I did in the war was hidden.

Valvis’s translation enjoys the endorsement of Papamarkos, who received the prestigious Academy of Athens award for Gjak. This English translation is the rightful winner of the Elizabeth Constantinides Translation Prize, given out by the Modern Greek Studies Association of North America. I fully expect that more accolades will follow for a translation so rich and so bold. Papamarkos’s stories have been adapted for the stage many times, and I anticipate that Gjak in translation will see successful production runs as well.

articles.title: Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or – a victory for sportsmanship over celebrity
articles.author: Josh Bland, Postdoctoral researcher of football cultures and heritage, Department of Archaeology, University of Cambridge
paras: First awarded by France Football magazine in 1956, the Ballon d’Or has grown from a relatively modest sporting honour into football’s most prestigious individual accolade. Its recent history has been dominated by the superstar rivalry between Argentina’s Lionel Messi and Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo, who combined have won 13 Ballon d'Or awards between 2008 and 2023.

I hate what it has become. The glitz and glamour. The simpering, Oscar-esque campaigning. Above all, I hate how it reduces football, that most beautiful of collective endeavours, to a procession of individual superstars competing for their place in some manufactured celebrity hierarchy of greatness.

So imagine my surprise when I found myself lying in darkness, laptop propped on my chest, glued to the BBC’s coverage. And imagine my even greater astonishment when, as England’s Harry Kane was named this year’s men’s winner, I found myself experiencing a genuine swell of emotion.
Why had an award that seemed to embody everything I despised about modern football moved me so profoundly?

My research examines football support as a form of living cultural heritage. One of my central arguments is that football heritage is about far more than historic stadiums, trophies or great players immortalised in bronze.

Instead, heritage lives in the relationships, shared memories, traditions and values that supporters sustain and transmit across generations. Heritage, in other words, is not simply about celebrating what has gone before. It is about deciding what we value from the past and present, and what we want to carry into the future.

In this sense, Kane’s significance goes beyond sporting achievements or the memories he has created for football fans. The heroes we choose to celebrate help shape our understanding of what football represents, and what we believe it ought to be.

Kane’s win points towards the future of football I and many fans would like to see. We spend so much time worrying about what modern football is becoming, Harry Kane reminds us of what it can still be. And for one glorious evening, the qualities and values I cherish most in football seemed to have won too.
A different kind of footballing greatness

There’s no argument that in footballing terms, this award is utterly deserved. England’s all-time leading male goalscorer and Tottenham Hotspur’s greatest marksman, Kane is now also the first Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001. He is undoubtedly one of the greatest English footballers of all time.

Yet, statistics barely capture his brilliance. A genuine footballing artist, Kane combines terrifying finishing ability with exquisite technique, spatial awareness and an extraordinary passing range. His genius is understated: his trundling style makes his shattering performances of the last year for his current club Bayern Munich seem deceptively routine. His leadership style is through relentless self-improvement, personal discipline and an unwavering commitment to the collective cause.

We live in an era when football seems increasingly consumed by celebrity, conspicuous wealth and the relentless cultivation of personal brands. Take the two most awarded players in Ballon d'Or history. In 2025, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi earned an estimated US$120 million (£90 million) between them from off-field commercial activities alone.

But the consequences run deeper than money. My research looks into football supporters’ ideas of authenticity in the game. Speaking with fans, I have explored how the game’s transformation into a global entertainment product can leave supporters feeling marginalised. Traditionally, football has been an intergenerational cultural tradition rooted in collective identity, shared values and community relationships; however, it is increasingly repackaged around individual celebrity and consumption.
The danger is not commercialisation itself, but that football’s identity as an entertainment product increasingly threatens to overshadow its significance as a living cultural tradition.

Against this backdrop, Kane feels like a glorious throwback. Grounded, sensible, quietly charming and refreshingly unostentatious, he seems almost defiantly ordinary for someone possessing such extraordinary talents.

There was something wonderfully incongruous about watching him collect football’s most ostentatious individual award. His shiny-eyed awe, his impish grin, his apparent lack of interest in the celebrity circus surrounding this most deserved of accolades.
Kane has spent his career quietly perfecting his craft, allowing his football to speak more eloquently than any carefully cultivated public persona. He is no celebrity; he is a sportsman.

In his humility, professionalism, quiet leadership and extraordinary dedication to his craft, Kane embodies precisely the values I would love future generations of footballers and supporters to inherit. His Ballon d'Or victory is therefore a wonderfully paradoxical triumph: a seemingly old-fashioned footballer conquering the most conspicuous symbol of modern football’s celebrity culture.

articles.title: Gulliver’s Travels at 300: a satire of the Anglo-Irish and the folly of allegiance to empire
articles.author: Clíona Ó Gallchoir, Lecturer in English, University College Cork
paras: Gulliver’s Travels, first published on October 28 1726, is a masterpiece of satire that continues to have the power to provoke, to amuse, and to shock. Most readers familiar with it will know that its author, Jonathan Swift, was not only Irish-born but was Dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin when he wrote what is unquestionably his greatest work.
What they may not know, however, is that the text is shaped in fundamental ways by Swift’s experience as a member of Ireland’s Protestant elite.

This group was a minority whose identity was constructed on the assumption that they were to bring order and civilisation to a wild and benighted country. They believed they would “improve” Ireland through their superior grasp of reason and their cultivated manner of living.

This civilising mission was from the start complicated by the irreconcilable contradictions for Ireland’s Protestants, who originally described themselves as “the English people of Ireland”“. They believed their role was to represent and model a superior culture to the inhabitants of Ireland. But, as they discovered, living in Ireland meant accepting that they were in fact considered inferior themselves. As Swift’s contemporary William Molyneux acutely observed:

If the English in Ireland be treated as Englishmen, they will be Englishmen still in their hearts and inclinations, but if they be oppressed, they will turn Irish, for fellowship in suffering begets love and unites interests.

In his Drapier’s Letters, a series of political pamphlets published in 1724 as he was working on Gulliver’s Travels, Swift likewise expressed his frustration at the anomalous position and unstable status of the Anglo-Irish:
Am I a freeman in England, and do I become a slave in six hours by crossing the Channel?

The focus here on travel as the means by which a free man is transformed into a slave is suggestive of the extent to which the dizzying disorientation and defamiliarisation that characterises Gulliver’s Travels has its roots in the complexities of Swift’s Irish identity.

The increasingly popular genre of travel literature in the 18th century functioned, broadly speaking, to establish the perspectives of western European travellers as definitive and authoritative. In contrast, Gulliver’s Travels works to question and radically undermine that position.

Part I sees Gulliver as a giant in Lilliput, with much of the satirical humour generated by the fact that the tiny Lilliputians are unaware of the comic incongruity between their size and their sense of their own importance. The "most mighty Emperor of Lilliput” for example – who is about six inches tall – is described as the “delight and terror of the universe” whose dominions “extend five thousand blustrugs (about 12 miles in circumference) to the extremities of the globe”.

Although Gulliver’s size suggests that he’s in a dominant position relative to the Lilliputians, this dominance is undermined by the monstrous nature of his huge body. Fearing that simply satisfying his basic need for sustenance will drive their country to famine, the Lilliputians consider killing him. However, they decide against it on the grounds that his immense, rotting corpse would be a source of disease.

Part II then sees Gulliver utterly humbled and stripped of authority through the simple device of making him tiny in Brobdingnag, a world of giants. In this situation, it’s Gulliver who fails to recognise the absurd figure he presents as he seeks to convince the king of Brobdingnag of England’s greatness. The king’s damning response to his lengthy account is to pronounce the English “the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth”.

Swift’s savage delight in undermining English claims to power and superiority, driven by his experiences as a disenchanted member of the Irish Protestant establishment, is further emphasised in Part III. Here, he visits the flying island of Laputa, where commonsense has been abandoned in favour of the fanciful experiments developed by the “Academy of Projectors”. This group is a satiric take on England’s Royal Society, which was founded in London in 1660 with the aim of promoting scientific enquiry and “improving natural knowledge”.

Swift’s contempt for projectors (close in meaning to the modern word innovators or speculators) is also evident in his Modest Proposal (1729). In this satirical essay, the great innovation of the self-styled projector is to solve Ireland’s social and economic problems by selling its surplus infant population for human consumption.

The profoundly shocking conjunction of rational method and barbaric cruelty that characterises A Modest Proposal is foreshadowed in the final book of Gulliver’s Travels. In this conclusion, the Houyhnhnms, a race of hyper-rational horses, calmly deliberate whether or not to exterminate the Yahoos. This oppressed group are reluctantly recognised by Gulliver as human, but are treated as a bestial subspecies by their horse masters. This chilling episode is rendered all the more disturbing by Gulliver’s agonised unwillingness to acknowledge his kinship with the Yahoos, and his self-abasement to the Houyhnhnms.

Gulliver’s deranged insistence on identifying with the Houyhnhnms sees him, when he returns home, take to living alongside his horses rather than his own wife and children. Gulliver’s final madness can be read on one level as a metaphor of the Anglo-Irish dilemma – a portrayal of a colonial population that remains stubbornly allied with a power that actually despises and oppresses them. However, Swift’s achievement is much more far reaching than this.

His unique dual perspective within the prevailing power structures of his time enabled him to grasp the folly of believing that one frame of reference is the only one possible. It is this that makes Gulliver’s Travels vitally relevant to contemporary readers 300 years since its first publication.

articles.title: Nathaniel Hawthorne’s notebooks reveal the strange workings of his imagination
articles.author: Robert S. Levine, Distinguished University Professor of English, University of Maryland
paras: After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825, 21-year-old Nathaniel Hawthorne returned to his family home in Salem, Massachusetts, to live with his mother and two sisters.

Over the next two decades, the aspiring author took on just two short-term jobs. Otherwise, he spent much of his time as a recluse: reading, taking long walks in Salem, socializing with a small group of friends, and writing stories and sketches from the third-story bedroom of the home he called “Castle Dismal.” During that period and beyond, Hawthorne kept a series of notebooks, which scholars see as an important primary source for understanding the ideas and descriptions that informed his early writings and later novels.
Mainly, however, the notebooks served as a writer’s repository: Hawthorne could let his imagination wander freely without having to worry about being called unconventional, depressive or mad.

For over three decades as a Hawthorne scholar, I’ve used the notebooks – later titled “The American Notebooks” – to help me prepare editions and scholarly monographs. But I’ve long been intrigued by the notebooks’ shortest entries. Often no more than a single paragraph, they make up fewer than 10,000 of the 200,000 words found in “The American Notebooks.” They are weird and captivating, and in their own way seem like what we now call flash fiction or microfiction.

Hawthorne published collections of his tales and sketches in 1837 and 1846, which included such macabre and bleak tales: “Young Goodman Brown,” “The Minister’s Black Veil” and “The Birth-mark.” In 1850, at the age of 46, he published his first novel, “The Scarlet Letter,” which established him as one of the leading American writers of his day.

After Hawthorne’s death in 1864, his wife, Sophia, began transcribing “The American Notebooks” for The Atlantic Monthly. In the process, she grew fond of the fragments, likening them to sketches that bring us “so very near the creative soul of the artist.”
I have collected 200 of the most compelling of these fragments for an edition that was published by the Library of America in October 2026.
Consider the following fragment, which has no relation to anything that Hawthorne actually published:
“To have one event operate in several places – as, for example, if a man’s head were to be cut off in the town, men’s heads to drop off in several other towns.”

Phrased as if for a story that would never be written, this jotting, complete in itself, conjures an eerie world in which violence toward one person reverberates through other people in other places, leaving human bodies mysteriously linked.
In a fragment written in 1836, Hawthorne fantasizes about upending social conventions:

“Would it not be wiser for people to rejoice in all they now sorrow for? – and vice versa. To put on bridal garments at funerals, and mourning at weddings. For their friends to condole with them, when they attained riches or power, as only so much care added &c.”

Hawthorne never wrote a story about women wearing bridal garments at funerals. But the stand-alone fragment, in the seeming spirit of Franz Kafka’s surreal and unsettling fiction, links success to misery, and happiness to death.

That Hawthorne could be regarded as a precursor to Kafka, who wrote posthumously published fragments, was first articulated by the Argentinian modernist Jorge Luis Borges in his 1949 lecture “Nathaniel Hawthorne.” For Borges, Hawthorne prefigured Kafka in his commitment to “pure fantasies that do not look for a justification or moral and that seem to have no other substance than an obscure terror.”
Borges’ assessment seems especially apt for the parables, fantasies and fragments that can be found in Hawthorne’s “American Notebooks,” many of which evoke a hidden menace or unsettling plot:

“A stove possessed by a Devil.” “Follow out the fantasy of a person’s taking his life by installments, instead of at one payment – say ten years of life alternately with ten years of suspended animation.” “Little gnomes dwelling in hollow teeth; they find a tooth that has been plugged with gold, and it serves them as a gold mine.”
In a longer fragment, written in 1853, Hawthorne anticipates the many horror films featuring a demonic or possessed child:

“A family, consisting of a father, mother, and two children, are out for a walk, and sitting together in a wood. The little girl rambles away into the wood – they call for her – within a brief time, she comes back. At first, they notice no difference in her; but by degrees, they begin to see something odd – they notice more and more, till, in the course of years, they almost suspect that it was not their own child, but a strange child, who came back.”

Hawthorne, who had two daughters and a son, captures how children can seem to their parents like mysterious little people beyond their control. He would explore this dynamic in Pearl, the willful child in “The Scarlet Letter.” At one point, Pearl’s mother, Hester Prynne, wonders whether she’s a “demon offspring.”

Hawthorne’s notebook fragments are wide-ranging, but certain themes repeatedly crop up: the psychology of divided selves, tensions between men and women and even possibilities for a better world. As he hopefully imagines in a stand-alone fragment: “Cannon transformed to church-bells.”

Who was Hawthorne the writer? A neo-Puritan moralist? A social realist? A modernist? A romancer? The fragments complicate rather than answer such questions. In his preface to “The Scarlet Letter,” Hawthorne remarks on his desire to “keep the inmost Me behind its veil.”
But with the help of the fragments, we get behind the veil, at least a bit – and glimpse something like what Sophia believed was the spirit informing Hawthorne’s writing.

articles.title: Robert Eggers’s Werwulf: the real history of wolves and werewolves in medieval England
articles.author: Aleks Pluskowski, Professor of Medieval Archaeology, University of Reading
paras: Robert Eggers’s historical folk horror Werwulf will be in cinemas this winter. It’s set in 1305, when wolves still roamed parts of England. As they vanished from English shores due to sustained hunting, however, the werewolf myth moved abroad. The creature changed from a pitiable victim into a diabolical killer, before being rediscovered and reinvented by the Victorians.

In Eggers’s film, a hunter arrives in an English village to enlist local peasants in a wolf hunt declared by the king. The premise has a real historical basis, as the character appears to be inspired by Peter Corbet, a Shropshire baron of the Welsh Marches.

In 1281, Corbet was commissioned by Edward I to hunt and destroy all wolves within a cluster of counties bordering Wales, with the aid of the king’s bailiffs. Although the campaign is sometimes explained as an effort to protect England’s lucrative wool industry, Edward’s orders specified the crown’s hunting domains first and foremost. Surviving documentation from medieval Britain often places wolves within forests, chases and parks, where populations of deer were also concentrated.

The wolf population in Britain endured Corbet’s hunts, although the last ones are difficult to pin down. Young individuals could have dispersed into already “cleared” areas, and a pack was almost certainly present on the North York Moors at the end of the 14th century. It is thought they may also have lingered in the Scottish Highlands into the 18th century. Animal remains currently being investigated may yet help archaeologists refine that timeline.

Early on in Werwulf, one of the farmers enlisted in the wolf hunt turns out to be a werewolf. Medieval people did believe in this possibility. In his encyclopedic work Otia Imperialia (Recreation for an Emperor), published in 1211, the statesman and writer Gervase of Tilbury described men transforming into wolves in England in accordance with the phases of the moon.

Gervase presented this as a real occurrence, but there were also accounts of fictional werewolves. Texts circulating in England such as poet Marie de France’s Bisclavret (circa 1160-1175) and the French folk romance, Guillaume de Palerne (William of Palerne), from around 1350, show werewolves being incorporated into courtly storytelling.
These texts told tales of human nobles trapped in wolf form, more victims than monsters. Yet they drew their imaginative power from landscapes in which real wolves could be seen and heard.
From pitiable victim to devil’s agent

Wolves continued to be written about in negative terms long after their disappearance, while werewolves became increasingly associated with foreign lands. But werewolves were also changing character, from victims of misfortune to agents of Satan.

In 1590, a pamphlet was printed in London which described the life, trial and brutal execution of Peter Stumpp, a German man accused of being a werewolf. Stumpp, a farmer from Bedburg near Cologne, had allegedly made a pact with the devil and acquired a magical belt that enabled him to assume the form of a wolf. The pamphlet was translated and expanded from the German account by the writer George Bores.

Stump was not presented as a sympathetic human trapped in wolf form, but as a murderous sorcerer who killed people and livestock and committed sexual violence, incest and cannibalism. Foreign werewolves were not entirely new. The 12th-century writer Gerald of Wales had placed his compassionate werewolves in Ireland, but Stumpp’s diabolical werewolf was a different creature entirely.

The English pamphlet significantly expanded and sensationalised the account it was based on, resulting in a 21-page narrative with an eight-panel woodcut image showing Stumpp’s capture, trial and execution. It also went to considerable lengths to establish the credibility of its story, invoking witnesses and correspondence from Germany.
Stumpp’s case was one of at least 300 prosecutions of werewolfery which formed an occasional component of the much larger number of witchcraft trials in early modern Europe.

In Britain, wolves were not sufficiently embedded in everyday life to become part of witchcraft prosecutions. In Scotland, however, with its intense witch-hunting culture and a surviving wolf population, a 17th-century court record shows the term being used as an insult, although there were no prosecutions of werewolves. In this respect the presence of wolves alone cannot explain where such accusations arose.
Rediscovering the werewolf
With the end of witch hunting, the werewolf largely disappeared from Britain as a serious supernatural possibility.

Then in the 19th century, writers and antiquarians began recovering and reinventing werewolf lore as part of a wider fascination with the Middle Ages. Priest and hagiographer Sabine Baring-Gould’s Book of Were-Wolves (1865) is the best example of this process. He consolidated a huge body of werewolf lore for English-speaking readers, helping to establish the comparative tradition for later popular representations.

Hollywood later drew on this inheritance, but made the werewolf a sympathetic cursed victim again in The Wolf Man (1941), a figure closer to Bisclavret than to Stumpp. In his upcoming film, Eggers has claimed he has hit the reset button on the werewolf, presenting the story of a cursed man seeking salvation through love, a premise that also echoes the werewolves of medieval courtly literature.
Meanwhile, wolves are recolonising parts of continental Europe. There is also an ongoing discussion about their reintroduction to Britain.

What will happen if wolves return as free-living animals after centuries of imagining them through stories? Today we do not fear literal shape changers stalking our forests and moorlands. Yet popular culture gives animals enduring meanings. Just look at the influence of Little Red Riding Hood and the persistent “big bad wolf”.
Werwulf could be the next story to shape how we imagine wolves. If they do return, those meanings may influence how we live with them.

articles.title: Victorian spiritualism capitalised on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money
articles.author: James Cronin, Professor in Marketing and Consumer Culture Studies, Lancaster University
paras: Death has never entirely stopped the living from trying to continue a conversation with their loved ones.

Today, AI-powered deathbots and a growing range of “grief tech” bring to market several ways that consumers can recreate the voices of the deceased. They open new commercial opportunities and experiences alongside uncomfortable questions about whether grief should be profitable.

Yet long before AI made it possible to simulate (and charge a premium for) a familiar voice, the spiritualist movement that swept across Victorian Britain negotiated issues of credibility, authenticity and commercial exploitation while transforming one of humanity’s most enduring desires into something marketable.
Our research into the business history of spiritualism in 19th-century Britain suggests that the similarities go deeper than a shared fascination with communicating with the dead.

Victorian Britain is often remembered as an age of industrial progress, scientific discovery and astonishing feats of engineering. Department stores, arcades and luxury brands fed a growing appetite for shopping. Yet the Victorians were also fascinated by ghosts, the supernatural and the macabre.

These tendencies might first be written off as a contradiction – the perseverance of premodern supernaturalism among an increasingly modern society. But a closer look reveals that the technologies that transformed Victorian commerce and entertainment also helped make ghosts visible, reproducible and profitable.

Large-scale plate glass production, advances in illumination, and optical physics (the scientific study of how light behaves and interacts with matter around us) allowed for the staging of phantasmagorical illusions like Pepper’s Ghost, while photography could apparently capture the dead. Gothic fiction prospered and cheap paperbacks called penny dreadfuls traded heavily in tales of the strange, the sordid and the supernatural.

The supernatural was not simply surviving on the margins of industrial modernity; it was finding new opportunities within it. The philosopher Slavoj Žižek offers a useful explanation, arguing that societies are sustained partly through an “underside” of practices and desires that appears to contradict their official values.

This underside can provide outlets for what the official values exclude, helping people live with the wider social order. Žižek calls this the “obscene supplement”: the provocative and discomforting underbelly that a society struggles to acknowledge even while relying on it.
Victorian spiritualism helps us understand how this obscene supplement could become commercially productive.
The rise of modern spiritualism

Spiritualism is the belief that the dead can be contacted through people known as mediums. It emerged in the US in the late 1840s, following claims from self-styled mediums the Fox sisters that spirits communicated with them through mysterious knocks.

Spiritualism reached Britain through visiting American mediums. Seances, public demonstrations, specialist publications and objects such as “spirit cabinets” helped create a movement with its own celebrities and commercial networks.

An article appeared in The Times in 1872 expressing surprise that among “a generation which boasts itself to be one of exact science”, spiritualism had developed such interest. In our interpretation, spiritualism offered access to something apparently missing from a society increasingly focused on producing, acquiring and displaying “things”: evidence that there was more to life than the material world. Yet spiritualism seemed to make that offer through more things: paid encounters, purchasable photographs and advertised products.

This is where Žižek’s obscene supplement becomes revealing. A society’s apparent opposites can provide ways of living with its demands without fundamentally changing them. Spiritualism offered an escape from Victorian commercial culture while drawing people into new forms of consumption. Making that offer convincing required careful management.
Making the impossible marketable

Spiritualist publications warned that mediumship could not be bought. Nevertheless, mediums had livelihoods, publishers needed subscribers and organisers needed to cover costs. Mediumship was therefore presented as an exhausting and often dangerous duty whose selfless practitioners deserved to be paid fairly for their services.

To protect the movement’s brand, mediums such as Daniel Dunglas Home would publicly refuse direct payment for seances. Instead, he accepted gifts, hospitality, travel opportunities and material support from wealthy patrons, while other mediums requested expenses and a moderate fee proportionate to their clients’ means. Commerce became easier to accept when presented as support for a higher calling.

The same tension appeared in spiritualist publishing. Periodicals such as the Medium and Daybreak could devote their opening pages to condemning materialism and warning readers against excessive attachment to worldly possessions, only to fill their back pages with advertisements for dubious remedies, elixirs and quasi-scientific products marketed to those very readers. Spiritualism’s critique of consumer culture actually helped generate further opportunities for consumption.

Scientific credibility also required balancing. Spiritualists welcomed scientists’ involvement, approximated scientific and philosophical language, and used technical equipment to make extraordinary claims appear worthy of serious attention.

Photography was particularly useful. A supposedly objective technology could produce images presented as evidence of spirits. Its dependence on darkroom processes also supplied a useful analogy for why seances required darkness. An account in Medium and Daybreak described a photographic seance near Newcastle in 1880. The correspondent alludes to the importance of darkness, not to conceal any trickery but to mitigate the “trying effect of daylight” on ghosts’ “materialisation”.
The ghosts of Victorian capitalism still haunt us

The Victorian fascination with communicating beyond the grave may seem distant from our technologically sophisticated present. Yet contemporary forms of “digital necromancy” reveal a remarkably familiar tension: the desire to transcend the limits of human existence continues to generate new income streams.

As with Victorian mediums, today’s grief-tech entrepreneurs operate within a delicate relationship between emotional need, technological credibility and commercial legitimacy. The promise of connection may be sincerely offered and deeply meaningful to those who seek it, even as that same promise becomes a source of profit.
Perhaps this is the more unsettling legacy of Victorian spiritualism: desires that appear to challenge a society’s dominant values may, in fact, help sustain the very structures they seem to resist.
Rather than unsettling the established order, they can create new opportunities for its continued flourishing. The ghosts of Victorian capitalism, it seems, have never quite stopped doing business.

articles.title: Clayface tries to tap into the success of body horror but can’t reach the genre’s gory depths
articles.author: Matt Jacobsen, Senior Lecturer in Film History in the School of Society and Environment, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Several characters have worn the mantle of the villain Clayface in DC comics across eight decades – but the two most prominent must surely be Basil Karlo and Matt Hagen.

Karlo, the first Clayface, who debuted in June 1940, was a B-movie actor who had no superpowers but did have a thirst for blood and a penchant for crime. In the 1950s Batman adventures, Clayface reappeared in the shape of Matt Hagen, a treasure hunter whose accidental encounter with radioactive material gave him the power to transform into a lumbering mass of muddy goo with superhuman strength and the ability to shapeshift into any likeness.

Other comic book versions of Clayface have come and gone over the decades, but for his big screen debut DC has opted to bring back Matt Hagen once again. This time Clayface is centre stage in a supervillain origin story, with a generous helping of body horror – a sub genre that has enjoyed renewed popularity in recent years.

In the film’s contemporary reimagining, Hagen is a Hollywood actor whose career high is ended when his face is brutally disfigured by mobsters in revenge for sleeping with their gang boss’s girlfriend. A desperate Hagen decides to put himself forward as a human guinea pig for the testing of an experimental formula containing microscopic AI.

This treatment promises to regrow damaged cells and repair the body to its original form. At first the results are promising, but then, in response to emotional excitement – especially anger – his flesh begins to warp and take on an unpredictable life of its own.
Following the comics, Hagen learns to shift his malleable face to mimic others. He uses these new abilities in a gory revenge rampage on the gangsters that assaulted him and wrecked his career.

While Clayface doesn’t live up to its genre-bending promise of a comic book body horror, it’s not an unmitigated disaster. The film is entertaining and features enough imaginative sequences to forgive some of its more prosaic and one-dimensional aspects.

I was excited at the prospect of a supervillain story from writer and director Mike Flanagan. The horror impresario is responsible for some brilliant recent adaptations, including the peerless Haunting of Hill House for Netflix. I was also hugely impressed with his risk-taking, imaginative update of Stephen King’s debut novel Carrie. However, Flanagan stepped back from the lead writing role – likely because of scheduling conflicts with Carrie.

He retains a co-writing credit. But there’s little in this film that recalls Flanagan’s sensitivity for character and the nuanced dialogue of his best work. A full rewrite by British-Iranian screenwriter Hossein Amini (the excellent Drive, the not-so-excellent The Snowman) may be partly responsible for the film’s tonal uncertainty and an oddly noncommittal feel to much of the action.
The finished product seems to be grappling with the daring originality of its premise and the need for mainstream appeal.
A strong lead for thin material

That said, Clayface’s lead, Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, carries the weaker aspects of the script extremely well with an admirable commitment to his character’s horrific transformations. The film’s best scenes show Hagen confronting what could either be seen as an exciting new body with superhuman abilities or a terrifying total degeneration.

Harries’ energetic performance produces some memorable sequences where Hagen wrestles with his unruly body, the best of which features a battle to keep his dysfunctional, goopy eyelids from sealing shut. Prosthetic effects are blended effectively with CGI – and horror fans should enjoy the effort and commitment from both the actor and the effects crew.

There are distinct shades of Coralie Fargeat’s outrageous and brilliant mainstream body horror breakthrough The Substance (2024). Clayface shares that relentlessly gory film’s interest in the shallow vanity of celebrity and the lengths the protagonist goes to in order to preserve youth and beauty in a skin-deep world.

Also, the connection between Hagen’s emotional state and his progressively warping flesh results in an interesting exploration of male mental health and its impact on the physical body. That a supervillain origin story tackles these kinds of themes is in itself quite admirable.

Clayface also has strong echoes of David Cronenberg’s masterful and influential piece of body horror The Fly (1986). In this classic, Jeff Goldblum’s scientist accidentally splices his DNA with that of a housefly. His transformation begins as a thrilling set of new abilities before becoming a full bodily breakdown into a grotesque creature.
Clayface aims to tread similar terrain, but simply can’t replicate Cronenberg’s ability to walk the line between terror and wonder at the body’s strange transformations.

The main obstacle to Clayface’s success, however, is the surface-level characterisation and very basic sketching of the supporting ensemble of cliched and cartoonish mobster types. This is most glaring in the eye-rolling love story thrown in to encourage emotional connection with the central characters.

This is something The Fly managed to pull off around the horror as scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) and science journalist Veronica “Ronnie” Quaife (Geena Davis) fall in love and try to defy the odds stacked against them. Theirs is an incredibly convincing performance of chemistry, which was certainly helped by the fact the two actors were dating. Sadly, Clayface just can’t replicate it.

While Clayface’s goriest sequences are full of the imaginative horror that only an enthusiast of the genre could conceive, its dialogue and character remains thin. The movie offers neither the emotional nuance typical of Flanagan at his best nor leans knowingly into the over-the-top tropes of gangsters or the mythology of the comics.

Instead, Clayface falls in a passable middle ground that may be overly tame for horror fans accustomed to the wild spectacles of Fargeat and Cronenberg’s work while also being overly icky and violent for comic book film fans.

articles.title: London Film Festival round-up: a five-star weepie, a sweeping Spanish epic and a misspent youth in post-punk Manchester
articles.author: Louis Bayman, Associate Professor in Department of Film Studies, University of Southampton
paras: Every autumn, the British Film Institute celebrates the best in cinema with a ten-day festival in London and across the UK. This year showcased a slate of compelling films – some of which are exceptional and look certain to garner industry accolades in the coming year.

The big stand-out is Elsinore, which was presented in the opening gala screening. Directed by Simon Stone, the film is likely to be Britain’s main Oscars contender, with special recognition going to its star Andrew Scott.

Scott plays the Scottish actor Ian Charleson as he prepares for the 1989 National Theatre production of Hamlet. Charleson, best known for his 1981 role as the Olympic athlete Eric Liddell in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire, was seriously ill with Aids at the time. He died in January 1990, soon after completing the run.

Hamlet is famously a tragedy of self-doubt, and Elsinore thus lifts the conventional biopic contrast of public triumph with private tragedy by demonstrating the potential of drama to both express and elevate reality. Through his transcendentally emotional performance, Scott reveals an actor at the top of his game. Expect tears.
The festival’s closing gala The Debut provides a fitting bookend, with Jesse Eisenberg’s comedy of a timid housewife who belatedly finds her voice when auditioning for a community theatre musical.

Where Elsinore finds the tragic parallels between stage and life, The Debut offers the pleasures of theatre’s consoling fantasy. The film’s star, Julianne Moore, conveys the subtle gradations from fragility to strength in her character’s onstage transformation into a woman about to take control of her life.

The relationship of art to reality has a more political significance in another of the festival’s triumphs, La Bola Negra. Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s historical drama weaves together three timelines revolving around a frustrated playwright who has been left a mysterious document in the will of his estranged grandfather.

The film shifts between this story and that of his grandfather’s experience as a somewhat reluctant fighter for the fascist forces in the Spanish civil war, and then to a visualisation of a lost work, La Bola Negra, by gay socialist poet and playwright Federico García Lorca. Regarded as modern Spain’s most influential literary figure, the poet and dramatist was killed at the age of 38 by the fascists at the beginning of the war.

As well as historical periods, the film interweaves feelings of political commitment, queer desire, and poetic imagination, thereby intermingling visions of better futures, past possibilities, and the danger that we might lose what we hold most dear.

Behemoth! was one of the festival’s big Hollywood premieres, starring Pedro Pascal as a professional cellist and oddly passive Lothario. Its classical music milieu recalls 2022’s Tár, but Behemoth! is both far straighter and less weighty.

I enjoyed it as a film whose real star is its eclectic collage of musical genres that give rhythmic propulsion to its tale of an admittedly listless protagonist undergoing a midlife crisis. Although Pascal is the star, the show is stolen by an uproariously unhinged performance by Olivia Wilde.

Critics gave unanimous praise to Carol Morley’s semi-autobiographical depiction of post-punk Manchester, 7 Miles Out. But they reserved unanimous disdain for Klara and the Sun, an adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s speculative meditation on companionship, mortality and robot intelligence. Director Taika Waititi made the, shall we say, brave decision to translate the source novel’s compassionate understatement into whimsical farce, eschewing its sensitivity without any discernible gain in humour.

A few other films I found disappointing suggest a difficulty that contemporary culture has in narrating its own origin. One of these was Ink, Danny Boyle’s adaptation of the stage play charting the first year of Rupert Murdoch’s acquisition of The Sun newspaper.

This was undoubtedly a fateful moment in the making of modern Britain, but the film’s hyperactive visual style fails to make up for its attention deficits as it skirts everything from the decline of deference to the sexual revolution, trade union power, the morality of sensationalism, demagogic populism and a kidnap plot that merits a separate film of its own.
Such confusion also mars Primetime, a dramatisation of NBC’s reality series To Catch a Predator and its unscrupulous quest for top ratings.

Much slower than either of these, but also failing to live up to its own self-importance, is Fjord, Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner about a Romanian family that emigrates to Norway only to find their conservative religious beliefs punished by the self-styled liberal state.

A few films got the balance between dramatic depth and political breadth right. One is Artificial, which casts Andrew Garfield in the role of OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, portraying him as an evil schemer who sold artificial intelligence to the devil.

Another is Wild Horse Nine, a fictional black comedy from Martin McDonagh set in 1973 in pre-coup Chile. The plot revolves around a dysfunctional couple of CIA agents taking part in covert US operations to destabilise the Allende government. Played by Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich, the bickering agents take a trip to Easter Island so the elder of the pair can see the stone heads before he dies.

We can end however with a special commendation for a film whose depth is not achieved through the grandeur of its subject matter but its deliberate smallness. Korean director Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love begins with a documentary filmmaker assuring a sceptical producer that public interest exists for a film about corporate restructuring.

This opening forms in essence a bet that Possible Loves makes with its audience. The film follows the uneasy friendship between the documentarist and a working-class woman, its only plot point whether her monosyllabic and apparently violently troubled husband, who was laid off several years earlier, will consent to give an interview.

This deliberate smallness opens out onto the question of what remains when the great battle to save his job is long in the past, but whose resentment remains, determining family, class, friendship and self-worth in ways that are no less devastating for being intimately personal.
