articles.title: Moths in art history: centuries of creativity reveal the beauty of a misunderstood insect
articles.author: Samuel Shaw, Senior Lecturer in History of Art, The Open University
paras: Moths seem to be made for Halloween. They’re largely nocturnal, often outlandish in appearance and bear creepy names such as Lunar Thorn, Cloaked Carpet, Bordered Gothic and (best of all) Puss Moth.
The webs of the ermine moth caterpillar cover trees like ghostly shrouds, while the hairy caterpillars of the oak processionary moth release rash-inducing toxins.

Spookiest of all is the Death’s-head Hawk-moth, which bears a skull-like mark on its thorax and can squeak like a mouse. This is the moth that appears, albeit in altered form, on the poster for the film The Silence of the Lambs (1991).

Two historical prints held at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam speak to the long-held suspicion of moths within European society. In one work by the printmaker C. Galle, a group sets out with lamps to destroy moths before they can eat the crops (or produce caterpillars that do). In another, by Jan Luyken, women inspect the holes that moths have made in fabric. The Old English origins of the word “moth” denote a primarily destructive, parasitical creature.

Unlike butterflies (who doesn’t like butterflies?) humans have always found moths hard to love. I certainly didn’t give moths much consideration until this year, when I started researching representations of moths and spending time with the moths themselves. I’ve since become something of a moth evangelist.

From March of this year my son and I set up a Skinner moth trap in our small suburban garden in Leicester, rising early every morning to identify the moths that visited during the night. My expectations were low, especially in the first few weeks, when we caught little. But then May and June came, and every morning brought new gifts. My son took charge of the counting and by September we had identified a hundred different species.

If you think moths are all small, brown creatures, think again. Even in the UK, and despite their rapidly decreasing numbers, moths are astonishingly diverse and outstandingly beautiful, ranging widely in size, colour and temperament. Some of them – most famously, the luminously pink and green Elephant Hawk-moth – are disarmingly cute and docile and will happily sit on your hand.

The magic of moths has attracted artists for centuries. A good place to start is the Flemish artist Joris Hoefnagel (1542-1601), whose delicate watercolour sketches of moths remain astonishingly lifelike. I especially like his depiction of the furry Hummingbird Hawk-moth: one of a few day-flying moths and one of a few species benefiting from recent rises in temperature.

Even more astonishing is the work of the pioneering German naturalist and artist Maria Sibylla Merian (1647-1717), who published three books detailing the metamorphosis of butterflies and moths (or what she called “summer-birds” and “moth-birds”). Merian’s elegantly composed images were the first to situate moths within their wider environment, identifying which species preferred which plants.

Outside of the world of natural history, moths have tended to be given a marginal role. However, some artists have been as drawn to moths as moths are drawn to light. In 1959, for example, the Scottish artist John Maxwell (1905-1962) painted a series of colourful, abstracted moth paintings, including Night Flowers and Garden at Night (Moth).

Moths are especially well served by contemporary artists. The Peruvian contemporary artist Lorena Solís Bravo has considered the moth through the lens of queer ecology. Their 2024 film myth, moth, mother celebrates the mystery and transformative power of moths. The Devon-based printmaker Sarah Gillespie, meanwhile, has created a series of mesmerising mezzotint prints of moths. “I wasn’t looking for moths when I started drawing them around ten years ago,” Gillespie has explained “they came and found me. Their numbers may be in appalling decline but for me their presence has become ever more insistent”.

More recently, the artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg unveiled The Length of a Moment, three public sculptures at Oxford North, which visualise the flight of a moth interacting with the scent of a flower. Situated in an area rich with historic meadows, this artwork draws attention to diminishing moth populations and the need for better environmental management.

My favourite moth in art, however, comes courtesy of the 18th-century Indian artist Shaikh Zain al–Din. The moth that appears in his 1778 watercolour is the famous Death’s-head Hawk-moth. Here, however, it lacks the sinister and spectral nature of the moth from The Silence of the Lambs. Instead Shaikh Zain al–Din gives us a moth just going about its everyday (or every night?) business.

This isn’t the moth as a symbol of death, or as a muncher of clothes or crops (of the circa 2,500 species of moth found in the UK, only two actually eat clothes). This is a moth doing what moths do well: feeding from and pollinating plants, providing food for birds and looking rather beautiful while doing so. This image is a timely reminder that moths are much less weird and way more wonderful than most people think.

articles.title: The 90s: Art and Fashion Exhibition at Tate Britain – when rebellion became a brand
articles.author: Caterina Nirta, Associate Professor in Critical Theory, Royal Holloway, University of London
paras: Walking through Tate Britain’s exhibition The 90s: Art and Fashion, you recognise the images, the clothes and the curated disregard for respectability of those years. But like me, you might struggle to find the spirit of what made the decade matter.

Curated by former Vogue editor Edward Enninful, the show brings together many of the 1990s’ defining images, revealing how readily and comfortably the decade’s appetite for rebellion became a business plan. But the exhibition’s superficial and polished celebration leaves little room to ask what that rebellion actually changed, who benefited and who remained excluded.

Perhaps this failure suggests something the exhibition is reluctant to confront. The 1990s were the decade in which fashion and branding became extraordinarily effective at eating up whatever residual danger and urgency art still possessed, making provocation a currency for profitability.

This alliance between provocation and commercial value is captured by artist Sarah Lucas’s Chicken Knickers placed next to Kristen McMenamy No.3 by photographer Juergen Teller. Lucas’s photograph captures a raw, plucked chicken on a seemingly young female body. Teller’s image shows a woman smoking and looking at the camera wearing only “Versace” scrawled inside of a lipstick heart on her naked chest.

Together, these pieces show that a social critique of sexual objectification and branding can happily coexist in the same space. Fashion appropriated the visual language of feminist critique, using images that challenged conventional beauty and sexuality to attract attention and sell a look.

Increasingly, the promise of transgression provided a route into mainstream media. The capacity to disturb, however insincere, became an asset, and outrage acquired an audience that had already been trained to enjoy it.

The exhibition includes iconic work by photographers Corinne Day and Nigel Shafran whose unpolished, do-it-yourself approach helped shape the look of magazines such as The Face, i-D and Dazed & Confused (now just called Dazed).

Other photographs show super models stripped of their usual glamour in seemingly mundane moments. For instance, we see Ellen von Unwerth’s shot of Naomi Campbell sitting on a toilet in heels, shaving. Then there’s again Juergen Teller’s Young Pink Kate (main image), which presents a make-up free, ordinary-looking girl in bed with messy hair.

These images were an invitation to embrace our authentic selves and could feel liberating, suggesting that beauty did not require looking flawless. Yet their apparent ordinariness was carefully manufactured.

It’s also worth asking who was allowed to disregard beauty’s conventions. A young, thin woman could look scruffy and be praised for challenging expectations of feminine beauty. However, someone whose body fell outside fashion’s preferred shapes and sizes at the time continued to face hostility.

If there is one thing this exhibition shows, it’s that photographers, designers and brands acted as gatekeeper for the type of diversity that got to be celebrated. Designer Alexander McQueen’s minuscule corsets made of steel and wire exemplify that rigidity around a body, trapped and contained rather than liberated and celebrated.
Black excellence and the myth of Cool Britannia

The gallery dedicated to Black British artists offers a glimpse of what really happened behind the casual glamour of magazine covers. The fabricated myth of Cool Britannia with its promise of a young, creative and inclusive Britain, appears in all its shallowness contrasted against the horror of the racially motivated murder of 18-year old Stephen Lawrence in 1993.

Under the label of “Black excellence” is a quieter story of pressure, marginalisation and isolation. We see artists challenge forms of exclusion from British society through their work. Then when these same artists became successful we see their achievements collectively credited to British inclusivity. This is despite the fact that their work was calling out how exclusionary they found the country in the first place.

It’s difficult to reconcile this form of national storytelling with the outcome of the Stephen Lawrence public enquiry , which exposed a country where racism was deep-rooted in a national institution like the Metropolitan Police. Chris Ofili’s No Woman, No Cry artwork, a portrayal of Stephen Lawrence’s mother, Doreen, crying, is a reminder that we must individually confront what national celebration cannot repair.

Working on how people experience their bodies and how society treats them has made me particularly suspicious of the freedom we attribute to images. An unconventional identity could be celebrated in a magazine while the individual inhabiting that identity remains exposed to exclusion or violence.

For instance, queer visibility in fashion expanded in the 1990s and became profitable. However, this happened during a decade in which Section 28 continued to prohibit local authorities from “promoting homosexuality” and created a climate of fear around discussing same-sex relations in schools.
The 1990s commercial appetite for adventure and diversity co-existed with the decade’s wider reluctance to support truly adventurous lives.

The Tate exhibition has the ambition to be an archive of the decade. Like all archives, it operates by inclusion and exclusion. It authorises certain convenient narratives, hides what does not fit its storytelling and risks making the uncomfortable disappear into a story of linear progress.

Its failure to capture the true 1990s spirit stems from allowing insufficient room to examine the struggle over what those superficial pleasures really cost, who they served and whose lives they displaced.
The 90s: Art and Fashion is on at Tate Britain, London, until February 14 2027

articles.title: The Crucible: Arthur Miller’s morality tale was as much a reaction to his own marital failings as it was to the ‘red scare’
articles.author: Jan Machielsen, Reader in Early Modern History, History, Archaeology and Religion, Cardiff University
paras: Written at the height of the cold war “red scare”, Arthur Miller’s 1952 play The Crucible was a retelling of the 17th-century Salem witch trials (1692-93) which soon became the classic parable of mass hysteria.

Miller’s play has long been described as “a cornerstone of American theatre” and “an allegory of our times”. Adapted into a 1996 Oscar-nominated Hollywood film, recent stage revivals on Broadway (2016) and at the UK’s National Theatre (2022) further confirm its enduring popularity.

A staple of the high-school syllabus (a YouTube search yields over 3,200 school productions), the play has also come to shape popular understandings of early modern witchcraft. As Miller (1915-2005) foresaw, its interpretation of Salem became a flexible model applicable to other tragedies – so flexible, in fact, that “witch-hunt” has in recent years devolved into a virtually meaningless political catchphrase.

While acknowledging some artistic licence, Miller still claimed to have captured Salem’s “essential nature”, insisting that “the fate of each character is exactly that of his historical model”. As a work of history, however, The Crucible is deeply flawed; as a morality tale, it can even be described as positively harmful.

The central conflict driving the play – and the witch-hunt – is sparked by the illicit romance between John Proctor, an affluent householder, and his former teenage servant, Abigail Williams. As the witch-hunt unfolds, Abigail – described in the stage instructions as “a strikingly beautiful girl … with an endless capacity for dissembling” – feigns bewitchment and accuses Proctor’s suspicious wife Elizabeth (who had dismissed her from their service) in an apparent bid to take her place.

To save his wife and undermine Abigail’s credibility, Proctor confesses the affair. This gamble, however, spectacularly backfires when Elizabeth perjures herself, denying knowledge of the relationship to save her husband’s reputation – a dramatic twist that legitimises their servant’s accusations and seals their fate.

Notoriously, the Salem court executed only those who maintained their innocence. In the final act, Proctor is offered a reprieve if he confesses to witchcraft, but he dramatically refuses to lie: “How may I live without my name? … I have given you my soul; leave me my name!” With this final defiance, the flawed hero chooses death and redeems himself. To drive that point home, the play concludes with Elizabeth’s absolution: “He have his goodness now.”
In his 1987 autobiography Timebends, Miller described visiting “half-forsaken” Salem himself and going through the records and accounts in its Historical Society building.

“Almost every testimony I had read,” he recalled, “revealed the sexual theme, either open or barely concealed.” He found “hard evidence” of Abigail Williams’s “determination to get Elizabeth murdered”, recognising in one description “the joyous terror of the killer about to strike”. In a 1996 New Yorker article, he maintained again that “John Proctor had bedded Abigail”.

John Proctor was indeed one of the 19 victims of the Salem witch-hunt; Elizabeth survived the panic, her execution at first postponed because of a pregnancy. The real-life Proctor had also been a scathing critic of the court’s use of spectral evidence – the diabolical fits supposedly experienced by the child accusers.

This, however, is where the historical evidence and Miller’s drama diverge. Proctor was in his sixties, not in “his middle thirties”. Abigail Williams is presented as 17 in the play; she is played by a 24-year-old Winona Ryder on screen. Miller acknowledged that “Abigail’s age had been raised” but never stated by how much. Contemporary sources make clear that she was at most 12 years old. There is no evidence she was ever Proctor’s servant, let alone his lover.

All too often, when we study early modern witches, we see ourselves. Miller’s supposed “hard evidence” was little more than personal projection. In Timebends, the playwright admitted that he “had been searching a long time for a tragic hero”. In the New Yorker, he reflected how his own marital failings had caused him to empathise with Proctor:

My own marriage of 12 years was teetering and I knew more than I wished to know about where the blame lay. That John Proctor the sinner might overturn his paralysing personal guilt and become the most forthright voice against the madness around him was a reassurance to me, and, I suppose, an inspiration.
This relatable Proctor did not exist; Miller had invented him.

This points to two ways in which The Crucible is a deeply problematic work of fiction. First, by blaming the Salem tragedy on Abigail Williams, Miller roots a witch-hunt – of all things – in female malice. Second, by constructing Proctor as his hero, the playwright also employs the play and its supposed historic content as a vehicle for his own redemption.

Underpinning both distortions is a refusal to engage with the complexities of history. They show how easy and tempting it is to simply invert the original moral polarity, transforming not only accused witches into saints, but an allegedly bewitched child into a conniving teenage vixen.

Historians now recognise that many of Salem’s young accusers were deeply traumatised survivors of the Indian Wars (1688–1697); some even witnessed the brutal murder of their parents. Abigail, too, was orphaned, though the cause remains unknown.
Attributing blame and responsibility is rarely as straightforward as we would like it to be. Historical research requires careful study of both the evidence and our own biases.

The Crucible does not capture the “essential nature” of the Salem witch-hunt, but it does reveal a great deal about its mid-20th century author – and the anxieties, desires and misogyny that drove him.

articles.title: Hokusai’s Great Wave is one of 46 prints of Mount Fuji – seeing them together changes everything
articles.author: Dominik Havsteen-Franklin, Professor of Arts Psychotherapies & Creative Health, Brunel University of London
paras: When I first saw Katsushika Hokusai’s Clear Day with a Southern Breeze (also known as Red Fuji, 1830-1833), I was struck by its lustrous red resonating against the receding blue of the sky. Clouds align gently in an almost humorous formation. Near the peak of the mountain, are creases of snow. At its foot we are drawn to a multitude of tiny trees amassed in chorus. Easy to overlook, they change the picture. The great mountain becomes itself in relation to everything that surrounds it.

Dulwich Picture Gallery is showing all of Hokusai’s 36 Views of Mount Fuji, including ten added after the series became popular. Hokusai made them in his seventies in the early 1830s as cheap prints for ordinary people in Edo (today’s Tokyo). It is the first, and perhaps only, time the complete series will be shown together in the UK.

One image is instantly recognisable: The Great Wave (actually titled Under the Wave off Kanagawa). Seen alongside the others, it becomes one view among many – and a lesson in how quickly we settle on a single view of anything, including each other.

Three versions of Mount Fuji hang together in the first room. In Red Fuji the mountain is almost pure form. A light blue variant, its ridge edged in heavy indigo, opens a way into the mountain. A third, with lightning like cracks in a pot, feels dark and unsettled.

On the opposite wall hangs The Great Wave. Its foam reaches out like grasping, knuckled fingers, and flecks scatter across the dark water like stars in the night. Everything should be in motion, yet the print holds a stillness. Beneath the wave is Fuji again: a tiny triangle here where Red Fuji’s was expansive. It is the same mountain, but now framed by the sea.

Elsewhere, people hurry over bridges, work in fields and travel along roads. Hills seem to wear patterned bandanas of farmland, while Prussian blue skies fade at a soft, feathered edge. Shapes mingle playfully: three haystacks echo the three small peaks of Fuji’s summit. Hokusai places us in between, looking down on people and up at the sky, but never from a position that reveals everything.

In the third room, one print stopped me. In Mishima Pass in Kai Province, travellers link arms around an enormous tree. I saw an affectionate embrace, then learned they may be measuring its girth. How quickly I had decided what these strangers felt.

As an art psychotherapist, I work with exactly this. We imagine what others might be thinking and feeling, drawing on our own experience – therapists call this mentalising, and doing it well means staying with curiosity rather than assuming we know. I have never been to Japan and cannot experience Fuji as Hokusai’s first viewers did. What reaches me is what colour, form and shape do, across that distance.

Hokusai’s giant tree also recalls an experiment on awe in which people who had gazed up at towering eucalyptus trees for a minute picked up more of a researcher’s “accidentally” dropped pens than those who had looked at a building. A print may not make us kinder, but when we do feel part of a bigger picture, we may just become a bit less absorbed in ourselves, and perhaps more open to others.

The curation is less subtle than the prints. Its dusky blue walls echo Hokusai’s colours, but I was left cold. I felt fixed as a viewer, each picture held apart when I wanted to see how they connect – although the soft lighting creates an atmosphere, a quietness that simply lets you be with them.

At the end of the series, pilgrims climb into Fuji itself. Each looks much like the next, like frames of a stop-motion film. Near the summit they crowd into a shelter in the rock, a small window into something none could enter alone. We no longer look towards a distant mountain; we are drawn into it, among people making their own way upwards.

I left thinking about The Great Wave very differently. I could see the little mountain beneath it, but also the trees, travellers and pilgrims. The Fuji I began with had amassed a sense of journey, unfolding across the series.

articles.title: Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z’s weightlifting obsession – here’s why
articles.author: Claire Warden, Professor of Performance and Physical Culture, Loughborough University
paras: More than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out.

Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health.

People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras.
In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry.

As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French.

The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825.

The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century.

A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest.

But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted.

From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa.

Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training.
Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic.
Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake.
The post-war aerobics boom

The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity.

In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom.

New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing.
The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room.

In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it.
Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible.

Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies.
Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics.

By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok.

Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema.
Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm.

articles.title: What Fernando Botero’s exaggerated figures reveal about sex, power and violence
articles.author: Pippa Catterall, Professor of History and Policy, University of Westminster
paras: Opera Gallery London’s latest show is the first solo exhibition of the work of the Colombian artist Fernando Botero (1932-2023) in the city since 2015.

Fernando Botero, in Praise of an Amplified World presents a range of paintings and sculptures from across the artist’s 70-year career. The earliest works included date from the 1960s. The latest represent the remarkable material he continued to produce right up to his death aged 91 in 2023.

By the time the earliest work on display was painted, a self-portrait of himself aged one, painted when he was in his thirties in 1966, Botero had already developed the characteristic approach to depiction that was to become his hallmark.

Botero in 1992 explained away his distinctive way of playing with scale by saying that “an artist is attracted to certain types of form without knowing why. You adopt a position intuitively; it is only later that you try to rationalise or even justify it”. Botero’s rationalisation was that in 1957, when painting his groundbreaking work Bodegón con Mandolina (Still Life with Mandolin), he realised that changing the proportions of an object altered how it was perceived.

The resulting exaggerations of scale can be seen as humorous or playful. Yet there is much more to Botero’s art than that. Indeed, he developed a style known as Boterismo that used ample proportions to emphasise his themes, satirise and criticise, celebrate life and imbue the ordinary with a monumental quality.
After a move to Spain aged 20, Botero honed his craft by copying old masters in the Prado museum in Madrid. His art developed in dialogue with the masterpieces he observed.

Botero’s work frequently references and parodies historic artworks. In the process he also challenges the voyeuristic gaze. In contrast to the lavish settings sometimes used in historic works his voluptuously reclining women, such as Donna Sdraiata (2012), focus attention on the human form and represent womanliness rather than some form of idealised beauty.

Size is used repeatedly by Botero to subvert what we expect to see. He thereby draws our eyes to details that he wishes to emphasise, often the human aspect of the scene. Instead of using figures to give scale and meaning to the landscape, Botero centres them both in his depictions and titles. An example is his Concierto Campestre (Country Concert, 2017), dominated by a monumental courting couple. In a reversal of historic paintings, it is the landscape that is incidental.

To a British eye, the ample flesh of his subjects can seem reminiscent of the art of Beryl Cook, although Botero’s colour scheme is brighter, his pictures less comedic and his subjects more fully drawn. Somehow that colour enlivens his pictures, heightening the disruptive effects of his art on the viewer.

Take Girl with Cat (1989). Again, this responds to a theme often depicted in the past. Yet the monstrous proportions of both subjects are a world away from the Victorian sentimentalising or sexualising of young femininity. A painting we might expect to foreground either is rendered unsettling, while the almost human features of the cat contrast with girl’s and subvert our expectations. It is an arresting image.

So, more literally, is El Arrastre (The Drag, 1984). Ostensibly it depicts the process of dragging a dead bull out at the end of a bullfight. It is a sight Botero, who spent two years training to be a matador in his youth, was very familiar with. Yet it is the massive bull that dominates the painting in a manner reminiscent of historic death scenes of heroes, and not the tiny matador. Meanwhile, the dismounted picadors look less like bullfighters and more like brutal policemen.

Botero here references Francisco Goya’s work on bullfights to – like Goya – comment on human brutality to their fellow men, in this case in the context of the fighting and assassinations in the ongoing drugs war in Colombia that centred on his home city of Medellín.
This exhibition does not include much of Botero’s more political art, such as the Abu Ghraib paintings he angrily produced in response to the atrocities committed there following the 2003 Iraq war.

Yet there is throughout a dramatic tension both with the historic art and with contemporary politics. Prelados Bañándose en un Rio (1968) (Bathing Bishops in a River), for instance, references the contemporary second episcopal conference of Latin America in Medellín, enlivened by the first ever Papal visit to South America, by placing some Catholic bishops in a river, some fully submerged by the changes taking place in the church following Vatican II (the birth of liberation theology, which urged the church to become directly involved in the struggles of the poor).

Subverting the conventional image is also central to A Couple (2014). Contrary to what we might expect, it is the woman who stands towering over the seated man. Yet they hold hands, while on the table before them lie a slice of watermelon and two soft fruits, historic symbols of the female body and female sensuality. This is a depiction that foregrounds relationships and humanity, in contrast to the possessions or memento mori that sometimes throng the paintings that Botero is parodying.

Many of these paintings and sculptures are, like their subjects, monumental in scale. One that is not, among the latest work to be included, is Flautista (Flutist, 2023). Here again, disturbing differences in scale are used to make a serious point. The flute is too small and the hands too large. This absurdity satirises the pretensions of civility celebrated in artistic scenes of historic domesticity.
Like all Botero’s work, it is unsettling as well as sensual, playing with expectation of scale to force us to think about life as well as art.
Fernando Botero, in Praise of an Amplified World is at the Opera Gallery, London until November 22

articles.title: Autumn wreaths and ‘doorscaping’: why we need more life in our front gardens
articles.author: James Simpson, Lecturer in Landscape Architecture, University of Sheffield
paras: There was a time when decorative wreaths appeared on front doors in December, stayed on front doors for a few weeks, and then disappeared.
Now red and gold autumn wreaths and Halloween wreaths are popping up everywhere. These seasonal displays are part of a wider social media fashion for “doorscaping”.

It is easy to see the appeal. A wreath introduces colour, foliage and a little seasonal personality without much effort. But this enthusiasm for decorating the front door raises an interesting possibility: could it encourage people to pay more attention to the garden immediately below?

Choosing a wreath and choosing plants for a front garden can both be ways of making the entrance to a home more attractive. A study of 1,000 people in England found that creating something beautiful was one motivation for front gardening. People motivated by appearance also tended to have greener front gardens.
That does not mean wreath enthusiasts will necessarily become gardeners. But the same interest in seasonal colour and decoration could encourage some to try planting around their front door.
And British front gardens could benefit from more planting.

The Royal Horticultural Society’s 2025 mapping estimates that 55% of front-garden space in Britain is paved, compared with 36% of back-garden space. Earlier RHS research found that the proportion of completely paved front gardens tripled between 2005 and 2015, although subsequent surveys suggested some recovery in planting.

Parking is one reason. An Ipsos survey found that, among people with largely paved front gardens or driveways, 28% said they needed the space for cars, while 45% thought it was too small for plants. Front gardens also have to accommodate access, bins and the everyday demands of domestic life.
But the cumulative effect of paving matters. One driveway can seem negligible. A street of them is a landscape.

This is where the appeal of seasonal decoration becomes useful. The seasonal colours and foliage that make a wreath attractive could also be found in plants growing around the front door. Someone who enjoys decorating their entrance might also be tempted to extend that interest into the garden.

A reused container, a few bulbs or a hardy perennial can be an inexpensive starting point. The RHS recommends containers for completely paved spaces, as well as climbers for walls and plants for otherwise unused corners.

Living plants do require some care. Pots need watering, and not everyone has the time, confidence or physical ability to maintain a garden. But starting with a few manageable plants offers a way to try growing something without committing to a complete redesign.

There may also be opportunities to go further. A strip beside a driveway or an unused corner could provide space for plants. Where practical, a few paving slabs could also be lifted to make room for planting. Parking and greenery do not have to be mutually exclusive.

These changes offer more than decoration. Flowers can provide nectar for insects, while shrubs and hedges offer shelter for wildlife. Larger plants, particularly trees and climbers, can provide shade and help keep buildings cooler in summer. Unlike impermeable paving, exposed soil and properly designed permeable surfaces can also help rainwater soak into the ground.

A study of more than 900 sites in front and back gardens and streets across England and Wales assessed combinations of grass, hedges, trees, shrubs and container plants. It found that mixtures of different plants generally performed better across several environmental measures, such as cooling or flood control, than just one type.
A pot of flowers cannot provide all these benefits, but it can still support insects and introduce planting where paving and parking have left little growing space.

Those decisions matter for new housing too. The 2026 Building for a Healthy Life design toolkit, a government guide to the design of housing developments, encourages space for planting in the front of houses.

But having space for plants is only part of the picture. People also need a reason to grow something. And this brings us back to the wreath. Its appeal lies in how easily people can add colour and character to the front of their homes.

If even some of that enthusiasm extended from the door to a pot, a border or a climbing plant, our streets could become more attractive and better for wildlife. If that interest grew to include more trees, shrubs and planted ground, it could also help our neighbourhoods cope better with heat and heavy rain.
What starts as a little seasonal decoration might become a lasting interest in growing plants.

articles.title: Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity
articles.author: Wesleigh Gates, Ph.D. Candidate in Culture and Performance, University of California, Los Angeles
paras: Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “Leviticus” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy, was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “American Horror Story” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre.
But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment.

Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies. The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film.

But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers.

Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “Sleepaway Camp” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “The Silence of the Lambs” (1991).
Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall.
Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back?

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.
‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space
Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner
Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity
Horror against heteronormativity
Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre.

Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple.
Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex.
Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths.
Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies.

Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “body genre,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies.

In body horror, the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh, blood and guts. Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel.

Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.”
Questioning identification
Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity.

“How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place.

When I teach horror, my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them.

Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping, which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it.

Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society.
‘Disidentifying’ with horror

When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: disidentification. For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living.

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror. It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre. And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and behind the scenes.

But the queer characters in “Camp Miasma” – both in Schoenbrun’s film and in its fictional counterpart – still manage to connect with themselves and their bodies. And I think they do this not just by watching horror, but by watching themselves watch horror.

So perhaps the draw of horror for queer and trans people isn’t just that it lets them identify with onscreen monsters or victims of violence. It’s that it gives them the opportunity to reflect on these identifications – and to reject them or transform them.
In the process of finding meaning in horror’s monstrous worlds, queer and trans people tap into their own power to respond to the monstrous world around them.

articles.title: Parthenon marbles loan to Greece is not a simple solution – who gets control over objects?
articles.author: Stephan Blum, Research Associate, Institute for Prehistory and Early History and Medieval Archaeology, University of Tübingen
paras: European museums have become more willing to discuss the colonial histories of their collections. But acknowledging how an object entered a museum is not the same as questioning who should control it – or who gets to produce knowledge about the past.
Few antiquities are more recognisable or such enduring symbols of dispute over cultural heritage than the Parthenon marbles (447 BC to 432 BC) in London.

The marbles made their way to Britain through Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman court. Elgin removed about half of the Parthenon’s surviving marbles from the Athenian Acropolis in Greece between 1801 and 1812 under a disputed Ottoman permit, and sold them to the British government in 1816. The first official request for permanent repatriation was submitted to the British Museum by Greece in 1983 and the dispute has been ongoing.

In October 2026, George Osborne, chair of the British Museum, proposed an arrangement under which the marbles would spend periods in both Athens and London. Greece has consistently opposed any loan that leaves British ownership claims intact.
This article is part of our State of the Arts series. These articles tackle the challenges of the arts and heritage industry – and celebrate the wins, too.
When explanation becomes an endpoint

Provenance research, exhibitions and scholarly debate have made the history of collecting visible. This is progress, without which we cannot distinguish between forms of acquisition or make informed decisions about restitution. But there’s a danger in treating explanation as the endpoint of inquiry.

Once the circumstances of an acquisition are reconstructed, a contested object can appear to have been dealt with intellectually. So the object remains where it was, and the institution holding it retains authority over access, display and research.
The Parthenon marbles show the limits of this: we know a great deal about Elgin’s permit and its disputed wording, yet that knowledge has not settled who should decide their future.

Historical explanation can also manufacture historical distance – and distance is convenient. Take Troy’s Treasure of Priam, which the German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann smuggled out of the Ottoman Empire in 1873. This “acquisition” history is well documented, yet the finds, donated to Berlin, were looted by the Red Army and taken to the Soviet Union during the second world war. They continue to sit in a Moscow museum.

Germany has voiced claims for their return, but pursues them with little urgency, and the situation appears to have settled into acceptance. Whereas Turkey, where the objects were excavated, has little say at all despite wanting them back. In fact, the new Troy Museum has even set aside a room for them as a symbolic gesture, ready for their eventual return. But like Germany, they feel that Russia is never going to hand the objects back. So an account of past practices does not address their continuing consequences.

In many cases, the institutions that accumulated collections, archives, expertise and prestige under historic political arrangements still possess those resources today. However, historical circumstance should be part of the explanation, not a substitute for examining the present.
Legal is not the same as legitimate

And so, Greece seeks reunification of the Parthenon marbles but the British Museum argues that its acquisition was lawful under Ottoman authority, and that universal museums safeguard heritage for all of humanity.

The first claim concerns the 1800s. The question of who should hold the marbles concerns 2026. Legal continuity across two centuries of political transformation – the fall of an empire, the birth of a nation state – is not indisputable. It must be argued, not asserted.

The second claim, that universal access requires universal ownership, is also undercut by precedent. In 2023, the Vatican Museums gave three Parthenon fragments to Greece outright, rather than on loan, without any visible loss to either collection.

Also, a loan isn’t simply a practical solution to where objects should be exhibited. It sets the terms of the relationship. If a loan requires Greece to acknowledge British ownership, it asks the country seeking return to accept the very claim it disputes. One party holds the objects and dictates the conditions of their movement; the other must negotiate within a framework it rejects. Sharing access is not the same as sharing authority.

Another highly contested artefact is the bust of the Egyptian queen Nefertiti (1370 BC to 1330 BC). Discovered in 1912 during excavations at Amarna on the east bank of the Nile, the bust was allocated to the Germans under the partage system, which divided finds between the excavating parties. Egypt sought its return but negotiations broke down in 1933. The bust remains in Berlin.

The Nefertiti is often presented by Berlin’s museums as an ambassador of Egyptian art. The metaphor is revealing. An ambassador represents a country beyond its borders but the authority to appoint one should belong to the country represented. Who, then, has the authority to decide where Nefertiti should be?

The restitution debate often concentrates on the antiquities themselves. But who controls the archives? Who holds the laboratories, budgets and professorships? Whose interpretations dominate? Restitution that answers none of these questions changes less than it promises.

Alternatives already exist. In 2022, the German institution Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz transferred ownership of 512 Benin objects to Nigeria – roughly a third remain in Berlin on an initial ten-year loan. This proves that an institution can relinquish ownership without ending display or research collaboration.

The history of those objects – looted in the British expedition of 1897– differs from the Parthenon, Nefertiti and Treasure of Priam removals. Each case requires its own assessment. But the principle stands: retaining ownership is not the only way to preserve access.

The challenge for archaeology isn’t to become more critical of earlier generations, but to examine how the discipline’s structures shape the questions it asks and the answers it produces. That requires transparent provenance research, genuine collaboration with communities connected to contested collections, and a willingness to reconsider ownership where the evidence warrants it. Above all, it requires distinguishing between acknowledging an unequal past and changing the arrangements through which its consequences persist.

Archaeology knows how Nefertiti, the Treasure of Priam and the marbles came to be where they are. It’s been far less willing to ask why it remains certain institution’s right to send them anywhere at all. Until it does, the colonial past remains not invisible, but curated – explained in our exhibitions, governed on our terms.

articles.title: What faces in paintings can tell us about how we perceive emotion
articles.author: Zoe Thurtle, PhD Student in Cognitive Psychology, Sheffield Hallam University
paras: Look closely at a face in a painting and you might think you know what emotion the person is experiencing. A smile suggests happiness. A furrowed brow might signal anger. Widened eyes could mean fear or surprise. But what happens when you ask lots of people the same question? Do they see the same emotion, or something more complicated?
In our recent research, we tested how consistently people interpret faces and their emotions depicted in paintings.

Emotions are central to how we experience and navigate the world around us. Because facial expressions are an important way emotions are communicated, psychologists have spent decades studying what faces can tell us about emotional states.

One of the main tools for studying emotions has been photographic databases like the classic Pictures of Facial Affect. In these images, actors pose using standardised combinations of facial movements to represent six basic, widely recognised emotions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust and surprise. These passport photo type images are incredibly valuable for studying how people recognise clear, prototypical emotion expressions. However, expressions do not always fit neatly into one of these six categories.

To understand the more nuanced ways people interpret facial expressions, researchers also need examples that go beyond clear-cut expressions. However, asking someone to pose with a convincing layered emotional expression for a photograph is not straightforward.

So researchers have found examples from films or everyday life, while also introducing additional emotion labels and other ways of measuring how a facial expression is understood, such as how positive or negative and how strongly that emotion is felt.

I work as part of an international team of psychologists that decided to look at how art could offer a fascinating option. Take, for instance, Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa. There has been over 500 years of debate over whether she is smiling or not. Research has found that perceptions of her gaze can change depending on how the painting is viewed, and that her eyes can appear to smile even when viewed on their own. It is a striking example of how much information can be packed into a single painted face.
The face in a painting is the result of deliberate artistic decisions, observation and traditions, while tapping into the ways our faces naturally move when we express emotion.

In our research, we selected 116 faces from European paintings dating from around 1400 to 1900. Before testing, we standardised the images by making sure that all faces were clearly visible and similar in how they were positioned. We then cropped the faces from the paintings, removing the wider scene and body language so that participants were judging the expressions themselves. We presented these isolated faces to 152 participants, who viewed them individually and selected which of the six basic emotions best described the expression.

Our findings revealed that agreement exists on a sliding scale. On one end of this spectrum, some faces produced a clear consensus: viewers consistently selected the exact same emotion. We classified 61 of the 116 faces in this way as showing a classic “basic emotion”.
But the other 55 faces produced consistent patterns of responses across two or three emotional categories.

One painting that garnered such a response was Joan of Arc by Jules Bastien-Lepage (1879). The painting shows Joan in her family home in Domrémy, France at the moment she is told by the saints she must fight against the English in the Hundred Years War.

The full scene, along with our cultural knowledge of who she is and the heavy fate awaiting her, provides a vivid narrative context that helps us decode her psychological state. The chair beside her spinning wheel is upturned, telling us that she has been suddenly interrupted. When we look to the trees, we see the faint traces of the apparitions of the saints who have assigned her the terrifying burden of the role she must play in the defence of France.

But when the context was stripped away and participants viewed Joan’s isolated face, they didn’t agree on one single emotion. People most often saw fear, but many also saw sadness or surprise. For the participants, Joan’s expression did not convey a single, flat emotion but several plausible interpretations at once.

These complex, yet non-random patterns of response, to Joan’s face and the other 54 paintings, suggest that paintings offer interesting new avenues for the exploration of how people perceive emotion. Artworks then could offer researchers a wider range of facial expressions to investigate.

articles.title: Horror films exploit how human vision works to deliver movies’ best scares
articles.author: Arryn Robbins, Assistant Professor of Psychology, University of Richmond
paras: This article contains spoilers from popular horror movies and shows.

Imagine you’re in the movie theater watching 2018’s “Hereditary.” During one of the film’s most unsettling sequences, the main character, Peter, wakes up in bed disoriented. As he sits up, you hear a couple of gasps from others in the audience. The camera stays locked on Peter as he moves through his house and enters the dim living room.

You hear it again: more gasps. The lighting is low, a droning score builds tension, and your heart rate climbs. The people around you continue to audibly react. You haven’t seen anything scary yet, so what is everyone else responding to?
The camera slowly pulls back, and then you see her: Annie, Peter’s possessed mother, crouched on the ceiling in an unnatural way.
Watch the scene again and you might notice that Annie was in the shadows on the ceiling the whole time, following Peter through the house.
How could you have missed a human being on the ceiling, in plain view?

As a cognitive psychologist who studies visual perception, I’ve noticed that horror movies often exploit the gap between what’s in front of your eyes and what you consciously see. Directors and cinematographers act like folk cognitive psychologists, intuitively drawing your attention exactly where it needs to be to create a scare.
Horror movie fans have pointed out numerous examples of spooky figures and other unnoticed details in the background of scenes.

These blind spots exist because your visual system can’t process everything in a scene at once. You extract detailed information only from wherever your attention is directed. Anything outside the spotlight of your attention may go unnoticed, no matter how strange.

Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice something in plain view because your attention is engaged elsewhere; it’s the phenomenon behind the infamous invisible gorilla experiment, in which about half of participants busy counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit strolling through the middle of the game.

Horror leans on inattentional blindness frequently, from the ghost boy in “Insidious” to the background ghosts scattered through Netflix’s “The Haunting of Hill House.” Something is plainly visible, though you often don’t notice it until a rewatch, and this delayed discovery can make the scene even creepier.

A related effect, change blindness, is the failure to notice something changing right in front of you. The difference can be as simple as a shirt color, or something drastic like the possessed girl Janet in “The Conjuring 2” morphing into an old man during her interview with Ed Warren. The camera stays on Ed while Janet sits slightly blurred in the background, making the transformation easy to miss until she abruptly changes back.
Directors also steer your attention to set up a scare, pulling your focus away from something creepy, or putting it in exactly the right spot just before a jump scare.

Eyeline match is a perfect example of this strategy. In “The Conjuring,” a girl sits up in bed, her fearful eyes fixed upward. The film cuts to reveal she’s staring at the ghost Bathsheba, crouched atop a wardrobe.

This editing technique works because it’s similar to something your visual system does: When someone near you looks sharply in one direction, your eyes follow automatically. Psychologists call this tendency gaze cueing, a reliable effect in attention research. Editing just mimics the real-life version to create tension, which resolves the moment you finally see what the character sees.

Sometimes directors do the opposite, giving your attention nothing to follow at all. The opening sequence of “It Follows” is a wide shot of a panicked girl running in and out of her house. With no eyeline or cut to guide you, the wide framing forces you into visual search, scanning corner to corner for a danger that may not even be there yet. Will something appear in a window? Follow her out the door? The uncertainty and the search build the tension.
The split between detecting and identifying

Your visual field isn’t equally good at everything: Some parts of your visual system perform the initial detection, others identify what was detected. For example, the fovea, a tiny pit in the retina that processes the spot you’re looking directly at, contains photoreceptors called cones that process fine detail and color.

Beyond that central spot is your peripheral vision, dominated by photoreceptors called rods that are sensitive to motion and low light rather than detail. In a sense, your peripheral vision is set up to help you quickly answer the question “Did something just move?”

When there’s motion at the edge of your vision, your peripheral system detects it almost instantly. Your eyes make a saccade – a rapid eye movement – to place the fovea onto the target to identify it. That gap between detecting and identifying can create a feeling of unease because something registered, something is there, but you can’t yet say what.

Playing with peripheral vision is almost a trope in horror movies now. Think of any hallway or mirror scene where you’re focused on a character and something moves behind them, grabbing your attention before you can figure out what it is.
Faces where there are none
Human beings evolved to quickly detect, identify and respond to potential threats, such as moving animals. That’s one reason vision is so sensitive to detecting movement.

It also explains why people are prone to pareidolia: the human bias toward detecting faces even where none exist. Have you ever seen a face in your curtains or toast? Missing a real face is potentially far costlier than perceiving a fake one, so our brains likely evolved to respond even to patterns that vaguely resemble faces.

“Midsommar” exploits pareidolia directly. As Dani is carried toward the feast after her crowning as May Queen, viewers have noticed a face in the trees. “The Night House” uses a similar trick, where ambiguous object configurations resolve into figures and faces that capture your attention. The 1963 film “The Haunting” does the same with a wall pattern during a particularly creepy scene.

Directors decide what you get to see and what they leave hidden, from ambiguous shapes to sudden movements to shadowy figures in the background. They seem to understand how your visual system works, and they use this knowledge to create tension in that space between perception and recognition, as your brain tries to determine what, exactly, you’re seeing.

articles.title: When powerful women are remembered as witches, we should challenge the historical motive
articles.author: Lynsey Cowlishaw, PhD Candidate in History and Culture, Media and Creative Industries, King's College London
paras: Reclaiming the label “witch” has become an act of feminist solidarity. But are we recovering the women themselves, or a posthumous identity built from accusation rather than fact?

Historical novelist Philippa Gregory’s new novel Royal Witch arrives this autumn soon after the much-trumpeted release of Practical Magic 2, with Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman returning to our screens as the Owens sisters.
Both tap into something powerful in contemporary culture. The witch has been reclaimed as a feminist figure: independent, knowledgeable, bonded to other women, resistant to authority.

But as a historian interested in how women’s reputations change over time, I think our enthusiasm for reclaiming the witch comes with responsibility. Before we celebrate the label, we must ask why and from whence it came.

Royal Witch retells the story of Eleanor Cobham, a 15th-century woman whose extraordinary rise took her from relatively modest beginnings to the highest ranks of English power as Duchess of Gloucester, married to a man briefly heir presumptive to the throne (Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, uncle to the young Henry VI).

Then, in 1441, everything collapsed. A formal inquiry revealed that Eleanor had commissioned scholars to cast King Henry VI’s astrological chart and exposed her association with Margery Jourdemayne, the woman later notorious as the “Witch of Eye”. Eleanor was publicly humiliated, her marriage annulled and she was imprisoned for life.

It makes Gregory’s irresistible description of Eleanor, “the woman they called witch. Who would have called herself queen”, feel entirely natural. But the implied correlation between ambition and accusation is key. Eleanor belongs to a wider pattern in which the complicated political histories of powerful medieval women have gradually hardened into much simpler stories.

Take Joan of Navarre, another powerful medieval woman linked with witchcraft. A generation before Eleanor, Joan was the widow of Henry IV, stepmother to Henry V and to Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, and Eleanor’s stepmother-in-law.

Her fall from favour involved suspicions about split loyalties and the seizure of her dower lands. As the daughter of a French princess and the former Regent of Brittany, xenophobic doubt persisted throughout her later life in England. Yet Joan, an astute political leader, was never formally accused of witchcraft.

Joan’s reputation developed through association and repetition. Chroniclers introduced witchcraft into her story; later accounts repeated it, and her reputation became entangled with other supposed magical family members. The label travelled further than the complicated political reality. Historian Elena Woodacre captures that uncertainty in her biography’s title: Joan of Navarre: Infanta, Duchess, Queen, Witch? That question mark matters.

Gregory’s focus, Eleanor Cobham’s tale, is different, but the same flattening occurs. She had been lady-in-waiting to Humphrey’s first wife, Jacqueline of Hainault, before becoming his mistress and, after that marriage was annulled, his second wife.
In 1441, the crucial offence was not that Eleanor’s associates had cast Henry VI’s horoscope, but that they had done so without permission; that was the treasonous act.

As with Joan of Navarre, this only became a crisis because dismantling Eleanor’s power, and in turn Humphrey’s, had become politically expedient to those bringing the charges. With Joan, it was about her income and potential double-dealings. With Humphrey, his peace-leaning rivals used it to dismantle the duke’s aggressive war policy against France and permanently eliminate Eleanor and her husband as political players.

Three men, Roger Bolingbroke, Thomas Southwell and John Home, Eleanor’s chaplain, were indicted for treason alongside Eleanor. Their fates diverged: Bolingbroke was executed, Southwell died in the Tower before judgement, but Home was eventually pardoned. Eleanor was never tried by the secular courts that judged them, but faced an ecclesiastical process instead.
What stuck, in the end, was her own admission: that she had sought spells from Margery Jourdemayne.

Jourdemayne supplied remedies and was associated with fertility treatments among elite clientele, was well known at court and, it seems, well used by it. Once Eleanor’s household became politically dangerous, Jourdemayne’s existing reputation made her vulnerable. Eleanor survived. Jourdemayne was burned at Smithfield on 27 October 1441, the same day she was found guilty.

Over time, nuance and politics are obscured behind easy labels, such as “witch”, flattening context and shielding systemic perpetrators. This is how cultural memory works. The stories societies inherit are not static records of what happened. They travel between chroniclers, novelists, films and audiences, and even historians, accumulating and shedding meaning as they go, until the most memorable version becomes more familiar than the historical event itself.

The pattern is not unique to witchcraft or to Royal Witch. Discussing The White Queen series adapted for screen from Gregory’s Cousins’ War novels, literary scholar Misty Urban observed that modern retellings “attribute the same weapons to women that medieval authors did; they simply imagine a reception by the audience that is delighted rather than horrified”.
Those accusations – manipulation, ambition, occult influence – have not disappeared. We have simply learned to read them as evidence of power rather than proof of guilt.

Witch has now acquired another layer of meaning: a celebration of female knowledge, independence and resistance to patriarchal authority. That reclamation has value, but it is a different project from recovering the lives of historical women. If we collapse the two, we risk turning a misogynistic simplification into an empowering identity without asking whether it belonged to the woman at all.

That does not mean novelists should stop writing witches. Popular culture, Gregory’s novels included, keeps histories alive. I say this as a fan and fellow historical fiction author working in the same creative tradition. Engaging the public with the past is the core of what I do as a public historian.

But the question mark matters. Every generation inherits stories, and we also rewrite them. Historical women are remembered through reputations they never chose. We need not pass them on uncritically.
